practice_questions.text:
Which sociological perspective argues that social stratification is a universal necessity that ensures talented people fill the most important roles?
A) Marxist
B) Feminist
C) Functionalist
D) Interactionist
practice_questions.marks: C) Functionalist [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'false class consciousness'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that false class consciousness is a Marxist concept about working-class understanding; 1 mark for explaining that it describes a situation where the working class fails to recognise their own exploitation and accepts the existing social order as natural and inevitable. Example: 'False class consciousness is a Marxist term for the situation where members of the proletariat fail to recognise that they are being exploited by the bourgeoisie, instead accepting the unequal social order as fair or inevitable because ruling class ideology makes it appear natural.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one criticism of Davis and Moore's functionalist theory of stratification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a criticism (e.g. Tumin argued functional importance cannot be objectively measured; feminist critique that reward structures reflect gender bias; Marxist argument that stratification serves ruling-class interests). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Tumin argued that it is impossible to measure which roles are genuinely most functionally important to society. He noted that care workers and refuse collectors perform essential work yet are poorly rewarded compared with entertainers and senior executives, whose contribution to social survival is less obvious. This undermines Davis and Moore's claim that reward levels reflect functional necessity.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Weber's three-dimensional model of social stratification.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Students should include: Weber argued that stratification operates through three separate but related dimensions rather than the single economic dimension identified by Marx (1 mark); class refers to a person's market position and economic resources (1 mark); status refers to social prestige and honour, which does not always correspond to economic wealth (1 mark); party refers to organised political power and influence, giving groups the ability to pursue collective interests through action (1 mark). Any three of these points developed with an example earns full marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that social stratification benefits society as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two named perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: Davis and Moore's functionalist thesis is explained in depth — effective role allocation, performance linked to rewards, meritocracy, societal necessity. Contrasting: Marxist critique (stratification serves bourgeoisie, ruling class ideology, exploitation, false class consciousness) and/or feminist critique (patriarchy distorts reward structures independently of functional importance). Named sociologists used throughout. A supported judgement weighs the evidence and reaches a substantiated conclusion.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, clear judgement offered though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped; some named theorists; conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations of why inequality exists in modern society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments for and against a range of perspectives. Functionalist position (Davis and Moore) explained in depth: unequal rewards attached to functionally important roles, meritocracy, role allocation. At least two contrasting perspectives developed with equal depth: Marxist (bourgeoisie/proletariat relationship, exploitation, ruling class ideology, false class consciousness, two-class system); Weberian (three dimensions of class, status and party — social closure as a mechanism of exclusion beyond mere economics); feminist (Walby — patriarchy as an independent structural system, gender pay gap, historically male-defined functional importance). Named sociologists and concepts used throughout. A clear, supported judgement weighs the perspectives and reaches a substantiated conclusion about which best explains inequality in contemporary Britain.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present; both sides covered; named sociologists referenced; judgement at the end though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or two-sided but undeveloped; some named theorists; conclusion assertive rather than substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few or no named sociologists, little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a beanpole family?
A) A family with two parents and many children across two generations
B) A multi-generational family that is tall and narrow, with few children per generation but multiple generations alive simultaneously
C) A family formed when two adults with children from previous relationships combine households
D) A family in which grandparents, parents and children all live under the same roof
practice_questions.marks: B) A multi-generational family that is tall and narrow, with few children per generation but multiple generations alive simultaneously [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'cohabitation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it involves a couple living together; 1 mark for specifying that they are not married or in a civil partnership. Example: 'Cohabitation is an arrangement in which a couple lives together as partners without being married or in a civil partnership.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one global family form named in the GCSE Sociology specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming a global family form (polygamy/polygyny/polyandry, arranged marriage, one-child family policy in China). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Polygyny is a form of polygamy in which one man has multiple wives simultaneously. It is practised in some parts of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia and is associated with cultural and religious traditions in those regions. It is illegal in the UK. This shows that the nuclear family is not a universal or natural form but one among many arrangements found across human societies.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the beanpole family form and explain why it has become more common in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying the beanpole family (multi-generational, tall and narrow). 1 mark for describing its structural feature: few children per generation but multiple generations alive at the same time, creating strong vertical ties. 1 mark for explaining one demographic cause: declining birth rates mean fewer siblings and cousins (fewer horizontal ties). 1 mark for a second cause or development: increased life expectancy means three or four generations may be alive simultaneously, so grandparents and even great-grandparents remain active family members for longer.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that growing family diversity in the UK is a problem for society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more perspectives presented in detail with named sociologists, both sides of the debate covered, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a supported judgement. The New Right view (Murray) that lone parent families contribute to dependency culture, poverty and educational underachievement argues that diversity is a problem. Functionalist view that the nuclear family performs irreducible functions (Parsons: primary socialisation, personality stabilisation) also implies some concern about alternative forms. Counter-arguments: feminist view that diversity reflects women's growing economic independence; postmodernist view that individual choice is a defining feature of contemporary life; ONS data shows the nuclear family remains the most common form. Supported conclusion that weighs both sides.

Secure: Both sides present with at least one named sociologist. Judgement at the end though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided. Some named theorists. Conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, little judgement, few or no named sociologists.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that the nuclear family is the normal and most desirable family form in modern Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of perspectives for and against. For (the nuclear family as normal/desirable): functionalist view (Parsons) that the nuclear family is the most efficient unit for primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities; ONS data showing it remains the most common form; New Right (Murray) arguing that alternative forms, particularly lone parent families, are linked to social problems. Against: feminist critique (Oakley) that the nuclear family is a patriarchal institution exploiting women's unpaid labour; postmodernist view that diversity is a feature of contemporary life and no single form is superior; the existence of beanpole, reconstituted, same-sex and cohabiting families as equally valid forms; China's one-child policy showing family structures are politically constructed. At least two named sociologists developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary (family diversity, patriarchy, primary socialisation, dependency culture, beanpole family) used accurately. A clear, supported judgement that weighs the evidence.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or two-sided but undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive rather than substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, few or no named sociologists, little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the best sociological definition of deviance?
A) An act that breaks the criminal law
B) Any behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society
C) Behaviour that is harmful to other people
D) An act that results in a formal state punishment
practice_questions.marks: B) Any behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what sociologists mean by the term 'social construct'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a social construct is something created or defined by people in society rather than existing naturally or objectively. 1 mark for developing this: e.g. it varies across time, place or culture, so it is not fixed or universal. Full answer: a category or concept that is created and defined by people in society rather than being natural or objective, and which may change over time or differ between cultures.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way in which the definition of crime has changed over time in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an act whose legal status has changed over time (e.g. fox hunting with dogs; consensual sexual activity between adult men; marital rape). 2 marks for a developed description: explaining what the law was before, what it became and when the change occurred. Example: fox hunting with dogs was a lawful activity in England and Wales until the Hunting Act 2004 made it a criminal offence, demonstrating that the definition of crime is not fixed but shaped by changing social values and the exercise of political power.

practice_questions.text: Describe how two different sociological perspectives explain the social construction of crime.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per perspective. 1 mark for identifying the perspective's basic position; 1 mark for developing it with a named concept or sociologist. Acceptable pairs: Functionalist (crime defined by value consensus; Durkheim on boundary maintenance) + Marxist (law serves ruling-class/bourgeoisie interests, criminalises working-class acts while ignoring white-collar crime). Or: Feminist (law has historically encoded patriarchal values, e.g. late criminalisation of marital rape) + Interactionist (Becker's labelling theory, moral entrepreneurs, no act inherently criminal).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that what counts as criminal or deviant is shaped entirely by those with power in society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides of the debate addressed with named sociologists and sustained sociological vocabulary. In support: Marxist argument that the bourgeoisie shape the law to protect property and criminalise working-class behaviour; feminist argument that patriarchal power historically excluded harms against women from legal definition (e.g. marital rape); interactionist argument (Becker) that moral entrepreneurs with social power drive the labelling of certain acts as criminal. Qualifying or against: Functionalist view that crime is defined by value consensus reflecting the whole community's shared morality, not just elite interests; Durkheim's boundary maintenance function suggests legal definitions can serve broader social needs. Student cites at least two named sociologists, presents both sides, and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists present, judgement reached. Developing: One-sided or underdeveloped, some named theorists, conclusion assertive. Emerging: Basic descriptive points, few named sociologists, little evaluative judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that crime and deviance are always relative to the social context in which they occur.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against with at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. For the claim: interactionist evidence (Becker, Outsiders 1963) that deviance is not a quality of the act itself but is created by social reactions; historical variation (fox hunting, decriminalisation of consensual same-sex acts); cultural variation (alcohol, cannabis across jurisdictions); situational variation (self-defence vs murder). Against or qualifying: functionalist view that some acts (e.g. serious violence against persons) are universally condemned across cultures, suggesting a degree of universal moral consensus; Durkheim's value consensus implies stable moral boundaries, not pure relativism. Student weighs both sides and reaches a clear judgement about the extent to which relativism holds. Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement reached. Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist argued that education creates social solidarity by transmitting shared norms and values across generations?
A) Parsons
B) Bowles and Gintis
C) Durkheim
D) Becky Francis
practice_questions.marks: C) Durkheim [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'hidden curriculum'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the hidden curriculum consists of informal, unwritten lessons transmitted by schools alongside the formal curriculum; 1 mark for giving an example of what it teaches (e.g. obedience to authority, punctuality, acceptance of hierarchy, gender-appropriate behaviour). Example: 'The hidden curriculum refers to the implicit lessons schools transmit alongside timetabled subjects — such as obedience to authority, punctuality and acceptance of social hierarchies — that prepare pupils for their role in the wider society and workforce.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way in which functionalists argue education benefits society.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid function (e.g. creating social solidarity / transmitting norms and values / teaching specialist skills / meritocratic role allocation); 2 marks for a developed description naming a sociologist and explaining the mechanism. Example: 'Durkheim argued that education creates social solidarity by teaching pupils a shared history, language and culture. Through this process, children from different backgrounds come to see themselves as members of the same society, providing the shared identity that holds society together. Without this function, Durkheim argued, social cohesion would break down.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Bowles and Gintis's 'correspondence principle' and its implications for class inequality in education.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Point 1: Bowles and Gintis (Schooling in Capitalist America, 1976) argued that the organisation of schools mirrors the organisation of the capitalist workplace through the correspondence principle. In schools, pupils obey teachers, follow rules and accept hierarchies without question, just as workers must comply with managers in factories and offices. Point 2: The hidden curriculum transmits these lessons implicitly, leading working-class pupils to accept their subordinate position as natural. This reproduces class inequality by preparing each class for its designated role, while the appearance of meritocracy convinces pupils that unequal outcomes reflect individual ability rather than structural disadvantage. Links to named sociologists and clear explanation of the mechanism earn full marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that education primarily serves the interests of the ruling class rather than society as a whole.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): The response presents both sides of the debate with at least two named perspectives and sociologists developed in detail. Arguments supporting the view: Bowles and Gintis (Marxist) argue the correspondence principle and hidden curriculum reproduce class inequality; the appearance of meritocracy is ideology that legitimises unequal outcomes. Arguments against: Durkheim (functionalist) argues education creates social solidarity and transmits shared values that benefit all; Parsons argues meritocracy enables social mobility, allowing talented individuals from any background to achieve. Becky Francis (feminist) complicates the picture by arguing education serves patriarchal interests as much as class interests. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Supported judgement. Secure (5-7): Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present though development may be uneven. Developing (3-4): Relevant points but mostly one-sided or limited, some named theorists, conclusion present but assertive. Emerging (1-2): Basic points, mostly description, few or no named sociologists, little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that functionalist sociologists give the most convincing explanation of the role of education in society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of relevant arguments for and against. Arguments for: Durkheim shows how shared schooling creates the social solidarity and norms vital for social order; Parsons demonstrates how schools prepare individuals for adult society through meritocratic role allocation and the shift from particularistic to universalistic standards. Arguments against: Bowles and Gintis (Marxist) demonstrate through the correspondence principle that education reproduces class inequality rather than serving all equally; the hidden curriculum prepares working-class pupils for subordinate roles. Becky Francis (feminist) shows schools remain patriarchal institutions that reproduce gender inequality through differential teacher responses. Interactionists argue functionalists ignore the micro-level processes of labelling and self-fulfilling prophecy that shape individual outcomes. A clear, supported judgement that weighs whether the functionalist account is convincing given the counter-evidence from class and gender inequalities in outcomes. Comparison and contrast of perspectives is explicit. Secure (7-9): Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, clear judgement though development may be uneven. Developing (4-6): Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped, some named theorists, conclusion assertive. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, few or no named sociologists, little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the concept of a 'norm' in sociology?
A) A written law enforced by the state
B) An unwritten rule governing expected behaviour in a social situation
C) A shared belief about what is morally desirable in society
D) A formal reward given for conforming to social expectations
practice_questions.marks: B) An unwritten rule governing expected behaviour in a social situation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sanctions' as used in sociology.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that sanctions are rewards or punishments; 1 mark for indicating they are used to enforce norms or encourage conformity and discourage deviance. Example: 'Sanctions are rewards or punishments that societies use to enforce norms and encourage conformity; positive sanctions reward conformity while negative sanctions punish deviance.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one example of cultural diversity and describe what it tells sociologists about the nature of social norms.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant example of cultural diversity (e.g. differences in family forms between societies, varying dress codes linked to religious or cultural practices, contrasting attitudes to gender roles across cultures). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying that attitudes to gender roles vary significantly between societies (1 mark) and explaining that this shows norms are socially constructed rather than natural or universal — what is considered appropriate behaviour for men and women in one society may be regarded as deviant in another, demonstrating that norms are products of culture, not biology (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe what sociologists mean by the distinction between achieved status and ascribed status.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for describing achieved status: a social position earned through individual effort, qualifications or merit, such as the status of a doctor or a headteacher; it reflects choices and accomplishments the individual has made. Up to 2 marks for describing ascribed status: a social position assigned at birth based on characteristics over which the individual has no choice, such as gender, ethnicity or social class background; Marxists and feminists argue ascribed status creates structural inequality by privileging some groups over others regardless of ability.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that sociology is simply a more organised form of common sense.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The answer presents both sides. Arguments that sociology goes beyond common sense: it uses systematic evidence, theoretical frameworks (functionalism, Marxism, feminism, interactionism) and named research to challenge taken-for-granted assumptions; sociologists expose the social structures that produce outcomes common sense treats as natural (e.g. poverty, crime, inequality). Arguments that sociology and common sense overlap: everyday observation does inform sociological questions; some sociological findings confirm widely held beliefs. The answer names at least two sociological perspectives, uses key sociological vocabulary (social structure, norms, values, cultural diversity), and reaches a clear supported judgement. Sustained academic tone throughout.

Secure: Both sides of the debate addressed. At least one named perspective or concept cited. A judgement is reached but development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or descriptive. Some reference to sociological concepts. A conclusion is present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of what sociology is. Little engagement with the common sense comparison. Few or no sociological concepts. No clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that social structures determine individual behaviour and that individual agency plays little role in shaping social life.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for both sides. Arguments that structure dominates: Marxists argue the bourgeoisie's ownership of the means of production determines life chances; Parsons' functionalism sees individuals socialised into pre-existing roles; feminist analyses (e.g. Walby's six structures of patriarchy) show how institutions constrain women's choices across multiple social spheres. Arguments for agency: interactionists argue that individuals actively construct meaning in face-to-face interactions; even Willis's working-class 'lads' actively resisted school culture rather than passively accepting it. The answer compares at least two named perspectives, uses key vocabulary (social structure, agency, socialisation, patriarchy, false consciousness), weighs the evidence, and arrives at a reasoned and substantiated conclusion. Comparison and contrast of perspectives is explicit.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present; both sides covered; named sociologists/perspectives referenced; a clear judgement reached though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or two-sided but undeveloped; some named theorists; conclusion present but assertive rather than substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description; few or no named sociologists; little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist studied labelling of deviant pupils in classrooms in the study 'Deviance in Classrooms' (1975)?
A) Becker
B) Ball
C) Willis
D) Hargreaves
practice_questions.marks: D) Hargreaves [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'self-fulfilling prophecy' in the context of education.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the self-fulfilling prophecy involves a label causing changes in behaviour; 1 mark for explaining that this confirms the original prediction and distinguishing it from labelling itself. Example: 'The self-fulfilling prophecy is the process by which a label attached to a pupil — such as being told they are low ability — causes that pupil to behave in ways that confirm the label, so that the original prediction comes true, regardless of whether it was accurate at the start.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one finding from Hargreaves's study 'Deviance in Classrooms' (1975).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid finding (e.g. teachers rapidly formed stable assessments of pupils as deviant based on early interactions / labelled pupils were placed in lower streams / labelled pupils received less academic encouragement / the labelling process was self-reinforcing); 2 marks for a developed description explaining its significance. Example: 'Hargreaves found that teachers formed assessments of pupils as deviant based on limited early interactions, and these assessments became stable and resistant to change. Pupils labelled as troublemakers were then treated differently — placed in lower streams and subject to more discipline — regardless of their subsequent behaviour. Hargreaves located the source of deviant identity in the school itself rather than in the pupil's home background, a significant challenge to deficit explanations of underachievement.'

practice_questions.text: Describe what the hidden curriculum is and give two examples of what it teaches pupils.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Point 1: The hidden curriculum refers to the informal, unwritten lessons transmitted by schools alongside the formal timetable. Unlike the explicit curriculum (subjects and assessment), it is not deliberately taught but is transmitted through everyday school routines and organisation. Point 2: Examples include: pupils learn obedience to authority (sitting quietly, raising their hand, not questioning the teacher); they learn punctuality (being on time is enforced, lateness is punished); they learn to accept hierarchy (teacher above pupil, head teacher above teacher); they learn gendered behaviour (PE activities, seating arrangements). Bowles and Gintis argued these lessons correspond exactly to the discipline required in the capitalist workplace. Each point needs a named example and an explanation to earn full marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that what happens inside schools is more important than home background in explaining differences in educational achievement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Arguments supporting the view: interactionists argue that labelling by teachers (Hargreaves's deviant labelling, Becker's master status) and structural processes inside schools (Ball's Beachside — banding reflects and reinforces class) shape outcomes independently of home background; Willis shows counter-school culture is generated within the school context. Arguments against: Marxists argue in-school processes reflect wider class structures that originate outside school (Bowles and Gintis's correspondence principle is rooted in capitalism, not the classroom); Halsey shows class barriers exist before secondary school banding takes effect. At least two perspectives with named sociologists developed in detail. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Supported judgement weighing in-school versus out-of-school factors. Secure (5-7): Both sides covered, named sociologists, judgement present. Developing (3-4): One-sided or limited, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-2): Basic description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of the interactionist perspective in explaining educational inequality.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of arguments for and against. Arguments for interactionism: labelling theory (Hargreaves's Deviance in Classrooms; Becker's master status) explains how classroom processes produce unequal outcomes; Ball's Beachside shows banding as a micro-level mechanism of class reproduction; Willis's ethnography reveals how peer cultures develop inside schools. Arguments against: interactionism ignores macro-level causes — Bowles and Gintis (Marxist) argue inequality is rooted in capitalism, not teacher labels; Halsey shows class affects outcomes even before secondary school labelling can take effect; feminists argue patriarchal structures outside schools (Becky Francis) shape what happens inside them. A judgement that weighs whether interactionism is useful as a partial explanation, even if it does not capture the full picture of structural inequality. Comparison and contrast of perspectives is explicit. Secure (7-9): Most arguments present, named sociologists, clear judgement. Developing (4-6): Relevant but one-sided, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, few named sociologists, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of authority is based on formal rules and offices, where people obey the rules rather than the individual?
A) Traditional authority
B) Charismatic authority
C) Informal authority
D) Rational-legal authority
practice_questions.marks: D) Rational-legal authority [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'authority' as used by sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that authority involves the exercise of power; 1 mark for specifying that it is considered legitimate — people accept or recognise the right of the person or institution to exercise power over them. Example: 'Authority is the exercise of power that is accepted as legitimate by those over whom it is exercised, meaning people comply because they recognise the right of the authority figure or institution to issue commands rather than simply because they are forced to obey.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one of Weber's three types of authority.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming one of the three types (traditional, charismatic or rational-legal). 2 marks for a developed description of its source of legitimacy and a relevant example: e.g. 'Traditional authority is based on long-established custom and the inherited status of rulers — people obey because this is how authority has always operated, not because of any formal rule or personal quality. A UK example is the monarchy, where the Crown's legitimacy rests on hereditary succession over centuries rather than electoral mandate or personal charisma.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between formal and informal agencies of social control, using sociological examples.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Formal agencies of social control have official, legally defined powers — the police enforce criminal law, courts administer justice, schools exercise legal authority over attendance and discipline (1 mark, developed 2 marks). Informal agencies exercise control through norms, peer pressure and socialisation rather than legal compulsion — the family, peer groups and the media shape behaviour by rewarding conformity and stigmatising deviance (1 mark, developed 2 marks). Any two well-developed examples from different categories earn 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that power in modern British society is always exercised legitimately.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two named perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: Weber's analysis of rational-legal authority as resting on accepted formal rules and offices — in modern bureaucratic societies people broadly accept the authority of elected governments and legal systems. Functionalist view that authority structures serve the common good. Contrasting: Marxist view that authority ultimately serves bourgeois class interests, making it appear neutral via ideology; feminist view that patriarchal structures mean authority has historically excluded women and continues to reflect male-dominated norms. Named sociologists and concepts (rational-legal, traditional, charismatic, patriarchy, ruling class ideology) used throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped; some vocabulary; conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate Weber's theory of authority as an explanation of how power operates in modern society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Weber's three types explained and evaluated in depth — traditional (custom, monarchy), charismatic (personal qualities, instability), rational-legal (modern bureaucratic societies, offices not persons). Strengths of the Weberian framework: recognises diversity of authority types, explains how power is accepted beyond mere force. At least two contrasting critiques developed: Marxist critique (rational-legal authority obscures class basis of state power, ruling class ideology); feminist critique (all three types have historically maintained patriarchal power; Walby's state structure of patriarchy). Functionalist view also considered (authority as socially necessary). Named sociologists and precise vocabulary throughout. Supported judgement weighing Weber's framework against alternatives.

Secure: Most arguments present; both strengths and critiques of Weber; named sociologists; judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant but mostly descriptive of Weber without evaluation; some vocabulary; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of one type of authority; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a secondary agent of socialisation?
A) A child's immediate family
B) A parent teaching a child to speak
C) A school transmitting shared cultural values
D) A grandparent passing on family traditions
practice_questions.marks: C) A school transmitting shared cultural values [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'primary socialisation' as used in sociology.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating it takes place in early childhood (usually in the family); 1 mark for indicating it is where basic norms, values, language and a sense of identity are first learned. Example: 'Primary socialisation is the early childhood process, usually occurring within the family, in which children first learn the norms, values and language of their society and begin to develop their sense of identity.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one agent of secondary socialisation and describe how it shapes a young person's gender identity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an agent of secondary socialisation (school, peer group, mass media). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying the mass media (1 mark) and explaining that advertising, television and social media present narrow images of how men and women should look and behave, reinforcing traditional gender norms; feminist sociologists argue this socialises young people into accepting patriarchal expectations of femininity and masculinity as natural, when in fact they are socially constructed (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe how cases of feral children support the sociological argument that nurture is more important than nature in shaping human behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for describing a relevant case: e.g. Genie, discovered at age thirteen after extreme isolation, had not acquired language or normal social skills despite having the biological capacity to do so; years of subsequent support yielded only partial development. Up to 2 marks for drawing the sociological implication: feral children demonstrate that human biological potential for language, social interaction and cultural learning cannot be realised without active socialisation; without the social environment, norms and values are simply not transmitted, supporting the nurture argument that society, not biology, makes us who we are.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the family is the most important agent of socialisation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments supporting the family as most important: functionalists such as Parsons argue the family is the irreplaceable site of primary socialisation, transmitting core values in emotionally intimate relationships no other institution can replicate; primary socialisation shapes personality and identity before other agencies have influence. Arguments challenging this view: secondary agents (peer group, media) may be equally or more influential during adolescence; Willis's study shows peer groups can override family values; the media reaches individuals across all life stages and saturates identity formation; feminists such as Oakley note that families can transmit patriarchal norms as well as shared societal values. The answer names at least two perspectives/studies, uses sociological vocabulary, and reaches a clear supported judgement about the relative importance of agents.

Secure: Both sides covered; at least one named theorist or study cited; a judgement reached but development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped; some named concepts; conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging: Basic description of the family's role; little comparison with other agents; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that our identities are entirely shaped by the process of socialisation and that individuals have no real freedom to define themselves.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for both sides. Arguments that socialisation shapes identity: Parsons shows how the family transmits norms and roles to children who absorb them before they can critically evaluate them; structural perspectives (Marxism, feminism) show how class and gender positions constrain identity from birth regardless of individual choices; Oakley demonstrates how gendered socialisation begins at birth. Arguments for individual agency: interactionists argue individuals actively negotiate their identities in face-to-face interactions; Willis's 'lads' actively resisted the identities offered to them by school; modern sociology recognises that identity has become more fluid and negotiable in contemporary society. The answer compares at least two named perspectives, uses key vocabulary (primary socialisation, identity, agency, structure, patriarchy), weighs the evidence, and arrives at a supported conclusion that acknowledges the interplay of structure and agency.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present; both sides covered; named sociologists/perspectives referenced; a clear judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some named theorists; conclusion assertive rather than substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of socialisation; few named sociologists; little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologists identified five types of family diversity in Britain in 1982, arguing diversity is deeper than just different household structures?
A) Parsons and Murdock
B) Willmott and Young
C) The Rapoports
D) Oakley and Leonard
practice_questions.marks: C) The Rapoports [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'secularisation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a long-term process of decline; 1 mark for specifying that it involves a decline in the social and cultural influence of religion in society. Example: 'Secularisation is the long-term decline in the social and cultural influence of religion in a society, including reduced church attendance and weakening of religious authority over personal decisions such as marriage and divorce.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one of the Rapoports' five types of family diversity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming one of the five types (organisational, cultural, social class, life cycle, cohort). 2 marks for a developed description with an example: e.g. 'Cohort diversity refers to the differences between people born in different generations, who have experienced different historical conditions. Attitudes to divorce, cohabitation and same-sex partnerships differ markedly between older cohorts (who may hold more traditional views shaped by religion) and younger cohorts (for whom these arrangements are largely normal).'

practice_questions.text: Describe how the changing status of women has contributed to changes in family structures since the 1970s.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying women's growing participation in paid employment and economic independence. 1 mark for linking this to a change in family form: e.g. women's economic independence reduced financial dependence on male partners, contributing to rising divorce rates and the growth of lone parent families. 1 mark for a second link: the growth of dual career families as both partners work full-time. 1 mark for a further development or named sociologist: e.g. feminist sociologists such as Oakley argued that women's growing independence represented progress away from the patriarchal conventional family in which women's labour was unpaid and undervalued.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that secularisation is the most important reason for growing family diversity in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both sides of the argument presented with named sociologists and perspectives, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a supported judgement. For secularisation as most important: it removed the religious stigma from cohabitation, divorce and same-sex partnerships; without declining religious authority, legal changes such as the Civil Partnership Act 2004 would not have been politically possible; changing norms around marriage and divorce directly linked to falling church attendance. Against secularisation as the most important cause: feminist sociologists argue women's economic independence (Oakley) is the primary driver of rising divorce and lone parent families; economic factors (dual career families, housing costs) cannot be reduced to secularisation; the Rapoports' cohort diversity shows different generations carry different attitudes regardless of religion. Named sociologists developed in detail. Supported conclusion that weighs evidence.

Secure: Both sides present, at least one named sociologist, judgement at the end though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points, mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description. Few or no named sociologists. Little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that growing family diversity in the UK is evidence that traditional family values have broken down.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a clear supported judgement. For (breakdown of values): New Right (Murray) argues that growth of lone parent families and cohabitation is linked to poverty, crime and educational underachievement, representing a dependency culture; the Rapoports' cohort diversity shows that younger generations hold fundamentally different values to older generations. Against (not breakdown but change): feminist sociologists (Oakley) argue diversity reflects women's growing freedom rather than a breakdown; postmodernists see diversity and individual choice as features of contemporary society, not problems; statistical evidence (ONS) shows the nuclear family remains common, so diversity is addition not replacement; the five drivers of change (secularisation, feminism, economic change, technology, immigration) show structural causes, not moral failure. Sociological vocabulary (secularisation, cohabitation, serial monogamy, dependency culture, patriarchy, cohort diversity) used accurately. Comparison and contrast of perspectives is explicit. A substantiated conclusion.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present though development may be uneven.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or two-sided but undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, few or no named sociologists, little or no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of informal social control?
A) A judge sentencing an offender to a community service order
B) A police officer arresting a suspect under suspicion of theft
C) A parent setting a curfew for their teenage child
D) A prison officer supervising inmates during a work period
practice_questions.marks: C) A parent setting a curfew for their teenage child [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what sociologists mean by the term 'social control'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying social control as the mechanisms through which societies encourage conformity to norms and discourage deviant behaviour. 1 mark for distinguishing formal and informal forms, or for adding that it operates through both legal authority (formal) and everyday social interaction (informal). Full answer: the mechanisms, formal and informal, by which societies regulate behaviour and encourage conformity to norms and rules.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way in which religion acts as an agency of informal social control.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying religion as an informal agency of social control with a specific mechanism (e.g. religious moral codes, fear of social exclusion from a faith community, internalised religious values). 2 marks for a developed description explaining how this mechanism operates: e.g. religious communities promote shared moral expectations; members who deviate may face social disapproval or exclusion from the community, which acts as an informal negative sanction encouraging conformity without the involvement of legal authority.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a Marxist sociologist would explain the purpose of formal social control in a capitalist society.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying the Marxist perspective and its emphasis on class power. 1 mark for explaining that the police and courts serve the interests of the bourgeoisie rather than society as a whole. 1 mark for explaining that enforcement focuses on working-class crime (street theft, benefit fraud, disorder) while under-policing crimes of the powerful (corporate fraud, tax avoidance). 1 mark for the conclusion that formal social control reproduces and reinforces class inequality rather than serving a neutral social function.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that informal social control is more effective than formal social control in maintaining social order.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides of the debate addressed with named sociologists and sociological vocabulary, reaching a supported judgement. In support: functionalist argument that primary socialisation through the family internalises norms from birth, producing conformity without legal enforcement; peer pressure and social approval are constant and immediate reinforcers of behaviour; most people conform not because they fear the law but because they accept the norms of their social group. Against or qualifying: formal control is necessary when informal mechanisms fail or are absent; Marxist view that formal control protects ruling-class interests in ways informal mechanisms cannot; interactionist argument that formal labelling (court conviction) produces permanent consequences (master status) that informal sanctions cannot. Student names at least two perspectives or sociologists, presents both sides and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: both sides covered with named perspectives, judgement present. Developing: one-sided or underdeveloped, some theorists named. Emerging: basic descriptive points, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that social control serves the interests of all members of society equally.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. For the claim: functionalist view that formal and informal control maintain value consensus and social order that benefits everyone; Durkheim's boundary maintenance function suggests punishment reaffirms values shared by all. Against the claim: Marxist view that law and enforcement protect bourgeois property interests and disproportionately criminalise working-class behaviour; feminist view that informal control operates more intensively on women through patriarchal expectations in the family, in public spaces and in the workplace; interactionist view (Becker) that labelling and discretion produce unequal application of control across social groups. Student names at least Durkheim or Parsons alongside one conflict perspective, weighs the evidence and reaches a substantiated conclusion. Secure: most arguments present, both sides covered, judgement reached. Developing: relevant points but mostly one-sided, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic points, little evaluation, few named theorists.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist's 1992 study revisited affluent workers in Luton and found that embourgeoisement had not occurred?
A) Walby
B) Murray
C) Devine
D) Townsend
practice_questions.marks: C) Devine [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'institutional racism'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that institutional racism refers to racism within an organisation or system rather than by individuals alone; 1 mark for explaining that it describes collective failure of an organisation to provide equal treatment because of race, operating through processes, attitudes and behaviour. Example: 'Institutional racism is the collective failure of an organisation to provide an appropriate and professional service to people because of their race, detectable in processes, attitudes and behaviour that amount to discrimination even without deliberate intent by individual employees.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way the media contributes to inequality in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying one way (e.g. negative stereotyping of working-class people; under-representation or negative portrayal of ethnic minorities; limited or sexualised representations of women). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Media representations of working-class people often rely on negative stereotypes — portraying them as scroungers, criminals or socially dysfunctional. These representations can contribute to scapegoating, in which structural problems such as unemployment are blamed on the attitudes and behaviour of working-class individuals rather than on economic inequalities. This labelling process can reinforce existing inequalities by shaping public attitudes and policy responses.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Devine's key findings from her 1992 study of affluent workers.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Devine revisited Luton workers in the late 1980s, interviewing manual workers and their partners in the same location as Goldthorpe and Lockwood's original 1960s study (1 mark). She did not find evidence to support full embourgeoisement — workers had not absorbed middle-class values and abandoned working-class identity (1 mark). Workers retained a strong sense of class identity and resentment at extreme inequality despite rising living standards and consumer aspirations (1 mark). Many had lost faith in the Labour Party to deliver greater equality, but had not abandoned their sense of class identity or awareness of structural unfairness (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that class is the most important cause of inequality in modern Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: class inequality evidenced across domains (income, education, health, work); private schooling and old boys' network as mechanisms of social closure; Devine's finding that class identity persists; Marxist view of structural exploitation by bourgeoisie. Contrasting: feminist view that patriarchy is an independent system — gender inequality persists across all class levels (Walby); evidence of ethnic inequality through institutional racism; functionalist view that unequal outcomes reflect meritocratic differences in talent and effort. Named sociologists throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some vocabulary; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations of gender inequality in the contemporary UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Walby's feminist analysis presented in depth — six structures of patriarchy (paid work: glass ceiling and gender pay gap; household production: double shift; male violence; the state: under-representation); private vs public patriarchy shift. At least two contrasting perspectives developed: functionalist (gender role differences reflect functional specialisation, Parsons on expressive/instrumental roles — not necessarily oppressive); Marxist (gender inequality serves capitalism by dividing the working class and providing unpaid domestic labour, class conflict is fundamental). Evidence weighed: gender pay gap data, women's under-representation in senior roles, persistence of domestic labour inequality. Supported judgement about whether Walby's framework or alternative perspectives best explain gender inequality.

Secure: Walby explained with most arguments, contrasting perspective present, judgement offered.

Developing: Walby described but not evaluated; limited counter-perspective; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of gender inequality; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which age group is most overrepresented in official crime statistics in England and Wales?
A) 10 to 14 year olds
B) 15 to 24 year olds
C) 35 to 44 year olds
D) 55 year olds and over
practice_questions.marks: B) 15 to 24 year olds [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'white-collar crime'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that white-collar crime is committed by people in professional or business occupations. 1 mark for developing this: it is non-violent, often involves fraud, embezzlement or tax evasion, and is committed in the course of legitimate employment. Example: 'White-collar crime refers to non-violent offences committed by individuals in professional or high-status occupations, such as financial fraud, embezzlement or tax evasion, typically in the course of their employment.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one pattern in the relationship between gender and rates of criminal behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a clear pattern (e.g. men commit far more recorded crime than women; women are overrepresented as victims of domestic violence; women are overrepresented in shoplifting offences). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. men account for approximately three-quarters of all prosecutions in England and Wales; this gender gap is particularly marked for violent crime and acquisitive offences such as burglary and robbery; sociologists note that this pattern may partly reflect more intensive policing of male behaviour and that self-report data shows a smaller gap than official statistics suggest.

practice_questions.text: Describe what official statistics show about patterns of crime and social class.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying that working-class individuals are overrepresented in official crime statistics for street crime, theft and burglary. 1 mark for noting that white-collar and corporate crime (committed predominantly by higher-class individuals) are underrepresented or largely absent from official statistics. 1 mark for recognising a limitation: that the overrepresentation of working-class individuals may reflect policing priorities rather than higher actual offending. 1 mark for mentioning that self-report studies show offending is more evenly spread across social classes than official statistics suggest.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that official crime statistics provide an accurate picture of patterns of criminal behaviour in society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides addressed with named sociologists and sociological vocabulary, reaching a supported judgement. In support: official statistics are large-scale, nationally collected, and allow trends to be identified across time and social groups; they provide the only comprehensive record of crimes reported to the police. Against: the dark figure of crime means many offences are never recorded; interactionist perspective (Becker) argues statistics reflect policing activity rather than actual offending; Marxist view that white-collar and corporate crime is systematically undercounted while working-class crime is over-policed; feminist perspective that crimes against women (domestic violence, sexual assault) have especially large dark figures due to non-reporting. Student names at least two perspectives, presents both sides and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: both sides covered, named perspectives present, judgement reached. Developing: one-sided or underdeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic points, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that patterns of crime in official statistics are explained primarily by the actions of the criminal justice system rather than by actual differences in offending behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, clear supported judgement. For the claim: interactionist argument (Becker) that labelling and selective policing inflate certain groups' crime rates; institutional racism (Macpherson Report 1999) as evidence that police practices shape ethnic minority overrepresentation; self-report studies showing offending is more evenly spread across social groups than official data implies; white-collar crime evidence showing that powerful groups escape prosecution despite causing harm. Against the claim: real differences in material deprivation and social conditions do affect offending rates (structural accounts); the Crime Survey for England and Wales is independent of police recording and still shows some group differences; some patterns (age-crime curve) appear across all data sources and measurement approaches. Student weighs both sets of evidence and reaches a clear, reasoned conclusion. Secure: most arguments present, both sides covered, judgement reached. Developing: relevant points but mostly one-sided or underdeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic points, mostly description, few named theorists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which group consistently achieves below the national average at GCSE according to UK educational attainment data?
A) British Indian pupils
B) British Chinese pupils
C) Black Caribbean boys
D) Girls from professional family backgrounds
practice_questions.marks: C) Black Caribbean boys [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'attainment gap' as used in educational sociology.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it refers to a difference in average achievement between two groups; 1 mark for specifying that it is measured using examination results and used to document inequality between social groups. Example: 'The attainment gap refers to the consistent difference in average examination results between different social groups — such as working-class and middle-class pupils, or boys and girls — as measured by GCSE grades and other official statistics.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one pattern in educational achievement related to social class.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid class-based pattern (e.g. FSM pupils achieve lower grades on average than non-FSM pupils / working-class pupils are less likely to progress to university than middle-class pupils); 2 marks for a developed description using sociological vocabulary and noting the consistency of the pattern. Example: 'Pupils eligible for free school meals consistently achieve lower average GCSE grades than their non-FSM peers across every year of available data. This class-based attainment gap has persisted across different periods of educational policy, including comprehensive schooling and academy expansion, suggesting that structural factors outside school play a powerful role in determining outcomes.'

practice_questions.text: Describe how patterns of gender achievement in education have changed over time.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Point 1: Until the late 1980s, boys outperformed girls in public examinations. Since the 1990s, this pattern has reversed: girls now consistently achieve higher average GCSE grades than boys on most measures, particularly in English, languages and humanities. Point 2: The gender gap is not uniform. It is largest among working-class pupils, where working-class girls outperform working-class boys by a wider margin than the equivalent middle-class gap. This suggests that gender and class intersect: being both working-class and male is associated with the lowest average attainment, while gender advantage for girls is strongest in lower social class groups.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that social class is the most significant factor dividing educational achievement in contemporary Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): The response presents patterns of class-based attainment (FSM gap, university entry rates) alongside evidence that gender and ethnicity also produce significant gaps. Arguments for class primacy: class gap has been consistent across decades; Halsey's Origins and Destinations showed class barriers even before comprehensive schooling; Ball's research shows middle-class families use cultural capital in school choice. Arguments against or complicating: gender gap has reversed since the 1990s with girls outperforming boys — gender now produces its own significant gap; ethnic attainment shows patterns cutting across class (Chinese and Indian pupils perform highly regardless of class background). Intersection: class, gender and ethnicity are not independent but intersect. Named sociologists for the causal arguments (Halsey, Ball) and clear pattern descriptions. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Supported judgement. Secure (5-7): Both sides, named sociologists, judgement present. Developing (3-4): Mostly one dimension, some named sociologists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-2): Basic description, little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics as a source of data on educational achievement patterns.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of arguments for and against. Arguments for: official statistics (DfE data, National Pupil Database) are large-scale, covering all schools; they are longitudinal, allowing trend analysis over time; they are freely available and replicable, giving reliability. Halsey's Origins and Destinations used large-scale data to demonstrate persistent class barriers. Arguments against: official statistics are socially constructed — they reflect decisions about what to measure (grades rather than wellbeing, attendance, vocational outcomes); they cannot capture the processes that produce attainment gaps (labelling, hidden curriculum); league tables reward some schools over others in misleading ways; FSM as a proxy for class is imprecise. Interactionist critique: statistics describe patterns but cannot explain the micro-level processes of labelling and self-fulfilling prophecy that drive them. A judgement that weighs whether official statistics are useful for describing patterns even if insufficient for explaining them. Comparison of methods is explicit. Secure (7-9): Strengths and weaknesses covered, some named sociologists or studies, judgement present. Developing (4-6): One-sided, some relevant points, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description of one strength/weakness, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'segregated conjugal roles'?
A) Both partners share domestic tasks and leisure activities equally
B) Male and female partners have distinct, separate tasks — typically the man in paid work and the woman in domestic labour
C) One partner earns while the other manages the family finances
D) Roles are negotiated week by week depending on work schedules
practice_questions.marks: B) Male and female partners have distinct, separate tasks — typically the man in paid work and the woman in domestic labour [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'double shift'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it refers to women in paid employment; 1 mark for explaining that they also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home. Example: 'The double shift refers to the situation in which women who are in paid employment also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home, effectively working two shifts in a day.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the concept of the 'sandwich generation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the sandwich generation as middle-aged people responsible for caring for both their children and ageing parents simultaneously. 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'The combination of extended life expectancy (older parents living longer and needing care) and delayed childbearing (people having children later in life) means that many middle-aged adults find themselves simultaneously responsible for caring for dependent children and for their own elderly parents. This creates significant time and financial pressure, and the caring burden tends to fall disproportionately on women.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the functionalist view of conjugal roles within the family.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for naming Parsons and the functionalist perspective. 1 mark for describing the instrumental role (male breadwinner, financial provider). 1 mark for describing the expressive role (female homemaker and emotional carer). 1 mark for an explanation of why Parsons saw this as functional: the roles are complementary, not unequal — each is different but equally important, and together they meet the family's needs in a geographically mobile industrial economy.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that conjugal role relationships have become more equal in contemporary British families.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more contrasting perspectives developed with named sociologists, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a supported judgement. For growing equality: Willmott and Young's symmetrical family thesis (1973) — joint conjugal roles increasingly common through the principle of stratified diffusion; growth of dual career families; more men taking paternity leave. Against: Oakley's feminist critique — the domestic division of labour remains unequal; women perform the double shift or triple shift; decision making and money management favour men; the sandwich generation burden falls disproportionately on women. Parsons as context (functionalist endorsement of gender-divided roles). Supported conclusion.

Secure: Both sides present, at least one named sociologist, judgement at the end.

Developing: Relevant points, one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that the domestic division of labour remains fundamentally unequal between men and women in British families.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a clear supported judgement that weighs the evidence. For ongoing inequality: Oakley's research on housework (1974) — domestic division of labour unequal despite women's employment; the double and triple shift; research showing women in dual career households still perform more domestic tasks; the sandwich generation burden falling on women; decision making research showing men retain greater financial authority. Against (some movement towards equality): Willmott and Young (1973) — the symmetrical family and stratified diffusion suggest change is real; growth of dual career families; legal changes promoting gender equality. Parsons's functionalist argument as a descriptive starting point but challenged. Sociological vocabulary (segregated conjugal roles, symmetrical family, double shift, principle of stratified diffusion, patriarchy, conventional family) used accurately. Comparison and contrast of perspectives explicit. Substantiated conclusion that weighs the evidence.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociological perspective argues that society is held together by value consensus and that social institutions perform necessary functions for the benefit of all?
A) Marxism
B) Feminism
C) Functionalism
D) Interactionism
practice_questions.marks: C) Functionalism [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'patriarchy' as used by sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying patriarchy as a system involving male power or dominance; 1 mark for indicating it is structural and systematically disadvantages women in both public and private life. Example: 'Patriarchy is a social system in which men hold structural power over women, disadvantaging women across public spheres such as work and politics, and private spheres such as the family.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one feature of the interactionist perspective and describe how it differs from a structural perspective such as Marxism.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying an interactionist feature (e.g. focus on micro-level interactions, labelling, master status, self-fulfilling prophecy, subjective meaning). Up to 2 marks for a developed description of how it differs. Example: identifying Becker's concept of labelling (1 mark) and explaining that where Marxists explain educational underachievement by reference to the large-scale class structure and the correspondence principle (Bowles and Gintis), interactionists focus on how specific labels applied by individual teachers generate a self-fulfilling prophecy, explaining the same outcome through face-to-face processes rather than structural forces (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the key ideas of the Marxist perspective on how society works.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for describing class structure: society is divided between the bourgeoisie (who own the means of production) and the proletariat (who must sell their labour); the bourgeoisie exploit the proletariat by taking profit from workers' labour. Up to 2 marks for ideological control or false consciousness: the ruling class maintains dominance not only through economic power but by promoting ideas through education, media and religion that make exploitation appear natural; false consciousness prevents the working class from recognising their own position. Credit for naming Bowles and Gintis and the correspondence principle.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the Marxist perspective gives the most convincing account of how social institutions work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour: Marxists show how institutions (education, family, media) reproduce class inequality; Bowles and Gintis demonstrate the correspondence between school hierarchies and workplace hierarchies; evidence of persistent class-based attainment gaps supports structural analysis. Arguments against: functionalists argue institutions serve all of society, not just the ruling class; Davis and Moore's meritocracy model suggests inequality is functional; interactionists argue Marxism ignores individual agency and the role of labelling; feminists argue Marxism underplays gender as a structural force. The answer names at least two contrasting perspectives with named sociologists, uses sociological vocabulary, and reaches a clear supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one named contrasting perspective; a judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly descriptive of Marxism; some criticism noted but undeveloped; conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of Marxism; little comparison; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that the functionalist perspective is too conservative to explain the inequalities found in modern British society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of arguments for both sides. Arguments that functionalism is too conservative: it justifies inequality as functional (Davis and Moore) rather than exposing it as exploitative; Marxists (Bowles and Gintis) show institutions serve the ruling class, not society as a whole; feminists (Walby) show patriarchal structures are maintained by institutions functionalism treats as neutral; evidence of structural inequalities by class, gender and ethnicity challenges the notion of value consensus. Arguments that functionalism retains explanatory value: it explains social order and why most people most of the time follow norms; Parsons' analysis of primary socialisation explains cultural transmission; functionalists accept inequality exists and argue it performs a motivational function (Davis and Moore). The answer compares at least two named perspectives, uses key vocabulary (value consensus, false consciousness, patriarchy, correspondence principle), weighs both sides, and arrives at a clear supported conclusion.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present; both sides covered; named sociologists referenced; a clear judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some named theorists; conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description; few named sociologists; no clear judgement.

before.exam_tip_html: The 12-mark Evaluate question will often invite you to compare perspectives. The most common error is to describe all four perspectives without evaluating them — this caps you in the Developing tier. To reach Secure or Mastering, you must: compare (“Unlike functionalists, who argue…, Marxists contend…”), evaluate (“A limitation of the functionalist view is that it ignores…”), and judge (“On balance, the feminist perspective is more convincing because…”). Never describe all four perspectives as equally valid without explaining why you find one more or less convincing than another. The examiner is looking for a reasoned judgement, not a balanced description.

practice_questions.text:
Which term describes the knowledge, skills and behaviours that middle-class families possess, giving their children a systematic advantage in schools?
A) Material deprivation
B) Cultural deprivation
C) Cultural capital
D) Social cohesion
practice_questions.marks: C) Cultural capital [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'crisis of masculinity' as used to explain boys' underachievement.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the link between masculinity and de-industrialisation; 1 mark for explaining how this affects educational engagement.
