Example: 'The crisis of masculinity refers to the argument that the decline of traditional male manual industries left some working-class boys without a clear masculine identity that values academic achievement, causing them to see school success as incompatible with being male and leading to disengagement.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one finding from Halsey's research on class and educational achievement.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid finding (e.g. class remained a barrier despite comprehensive schooling / working-class pupils with similar ability were less likely to achieve high qualifications / meritocracy claim is challenged); 2 marks for a developed description explaining its significance. Example: 'Halsey's Origins and Destinations study found that even when pupils of similar measured academic ability were compared, those from working-class backgrounds were significantly less likely to gain high-level qualifications or enter university. This directly challenged the functionalist claim that education had become genuinely meritocratic after the introduction of comprehensive schooling, showing that class background remained a powerful barrier independent of ability.'

practice_questions.text: Describe how Ball's research showed that marketisation of education reinforces class inequality.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Point 1: Ball argued that the introduction of league tables and open enrolment created a system in which middle-class parents could use their cultural capital to advantage their children — reading league tables, visiting multiple schools, writing effective appeals and using social networks to access information about the best schools. Working-class parents care equally but lack the same resources, making parental choice less meaningful in practice. Point 2: Middle-class families can also move into the catchment areas of high-performing schools, a strategy that requires financial resources unavailable to most working-class families. Ball's research shows that market-based competition does not level the playing field; it gives already advantaged families further advantage, reinforcing rather than reducing class inequality.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that factors inside schools are more important than factors outside schools in explaining social class differences in achievement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Arguments for inside-school factors: labelling theory (Hargreaves, Becker) shows teachers create self-fulfilling prophecies; Ball's banding research at Beachside shows streaming as a mechanism of class reproduction inside schools; Willis shows counter-school culture generated in school context. Arguments for outside-school factors: material deprivation and cultural capital (Bourdieu) operate before the child reaches school; Halsey shows class barriers pre-date secondary banding; catchment area effects link school type to residential class segregation. Named sociologists from at least two perspectives. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Supported judgement weighing inside vs outside factors. Secure (5-7): Both sides covered, named sociologists, judgement present but uneven. Developing (3-4): Mostly one side, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-2): Basic description, little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations for the underachievement of some minority ethnic groups in UK schools.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of arguments for and against. Arguments using cultural deprivation thesis: some families transmit values misaligned with school expectations; language barriers may disadvantage some pupils. Arguments against cultural deprivation: it 'blames the victim', ignores structural causes, fails to explain why some groups with similar socio-economic profiles achieve differently. Structural explanations: ethnocentric curriculum marginalises minority ethnic pupils; institutional racism (embedded in school policies and practices, evidenced by disproportionate exclusions of Black Caribbean boys, Macpherson Report 1999); interactionist labelling by teachers shapes trajectories. Class intersection: class mediates ethnicity, so cultural explanations must account for working-class White boys who also underachieve. A clear judgement that weighs whether underachievement is best explained by family culture or by structural factors within schools. Comparison and contrast of perspectives is explicit. Secure (7-9): Most arguments present, named sociologists, judgement present. Developing (4-6): One-sided or undeveloped, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, few named sociologists, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which model of disability argues that disabled people are disadvantaged primarily by social barriers rather than by their individual impairment?
A) The medical model
B) The interactionist model
C) The social model
D) The functionalist model
practice_questions.marks: C) The social model [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'homophobia'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that homophobia involves prejudice or hostility; 1 mark for specifying that it is directed at people on the grounds of their sexuality, particularly lesbian, gay or bisexual people. Example: 'Homophobia is irrational fear, hatred or prejudice directed at people on the grounds of their sexuality, which can take the form of discrimination, harassment or hate crime against lesbian, gay or bisexual individuals.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the social model of disability.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the social model locates disability in society rather than in the individual. 2 marks for a developed description with an example: e.g. 'The social model of disability argues that it is not a person's physical impairment that disables them but the barriers society creates — inaccessible buildings, discriminatory attitudes and the absence of support. A person who uses a wheelchair is not disabled by their inability to walk but by the absence of ramps and lifts in public spaces. The solution, in this model, is to remove social barriers rather than to treat or fix the individual.'

practice_questions.text: Describe how ageism affects elderly people's life chances in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Ageism involves prejudice or discrimination on the grounds of age (1 mark). Older workers may be passed over for promotion or made redundant in favour of younger employees, reducing their earning power and economic security (1 mark). Older people on fixed pensions are more vulnerable to poverty, especially when living costs rise (1 mark). Under-representation of older people in elected politics means their interests in areas such as social care and healthcare funding may be under-prioritised (1 mark). Any three points developed with sociological vocabulary earn full marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that religious inequality in the UK is mainly the result of individual prejudice rather than structural factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the individual prejudice view: evidence of individual attitudes (surveys documenting antisemitic or Islamophobic views), individual acts of hate crime. Contrasting: structural and sociological account — employment discrimination studies showing systemic disadvantage for Muslim-named applicants; media stereotyping as a structural process that normalises prejudice; scapegoating as a social mechanism where structural economic problems are blamed on minority groups; labelling processes through which religious minorities are categorised and treated differently. Named processes (stereotyping, labelling, scapegoating, discrimination, Islamophobia, antisemitism) used precisely. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, key concepts used, judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some vocabulary; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of religious inequality; few sociological concepts; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that the social model of disability is more useful than the medical model for explaining the inequalities disabled people face.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Social model explained in depth — disability as social construction, barriers argument, solution lies in removing social barriers not fixing individuals; aligned with broader sociological principle that inequality is produced by social arrangements. Medical model explained — disability located in individual impairment, medical solution, historical context of institutionalisation and stigma. Arguments for the social model: evidence that the same impairment produces very different outcomes depending on social provision; disability employment gap reflects employer attitudes and inaccessible workplaces not just individual conditions; consistent with conflict perspectives (Marxism, feminism) that identify structural rather than individual causes. Arguments for the medical model's continued relevance: some conditions require medical intervention regardless of social provision; the model has enabled advances in treatment that improve quality of life. At least two sociological perspectives considered (interactionist on labelling and stigma; Marxist on how capitalism creates barriers; feminist on intersection of disability and gender). Supported judgement about the relative utility of each model.

Secure: Both models explained with most arguments; judgement offered; named concepts used.

Developing: Both models described but not fully evaluated; limited perspective application; weak conclusion.

Emerging: One model described; little evaluation; few sociological concepts.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist argued that the family serves capitalism by reproducing the workforce and absorbing worker discontent?
A) Talcott Parsons
B) Ann Oakley
C) Eli Zaretsky
D) Charles Murray
practice_questions.marks: C) Eli Zaretsky [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'primary socialisation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as the earliest/first stage of socialisation; 1 mark for explaining that it occurs within the family and involves children learning the basic norms and values of their society. Example: 'Primary socialisation is the earliest stage of socialisation, occurring within the family, through which children learn the basic norms and values of their society.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one feminist criticism of the functionalist view of the family.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a feminist criticism (e.g. the expressive role disguises unpaid domestic labour; the family serves men's interests not society's; the division of roles is patriarchal, not complementary). 2 marks for a developed description with a named feminist sociologist: e.g. 'Delphy and Leonard argued that the family is a patriarchal economic institution in which the husband is the head and chief beneficiary of all work performed within the household. Women's domestic labour — cooking, child care, emotional support — is systematically exploited for men's benefit. This means what Parsons described as the complementary expressive role is in practice a form of structural exploitation.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Zaretsky's Marxist view of the role of the family under capitalism.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for naming Zaretsky and identifying the Marxist perspective. 1 mark for one function: the family reproduces the labour force, with workers raising the next generation of workers at their own expense, subsidising capitalism. 1 mark for a second function: the family absorbs worker discontent, acting as an emotional refuge that reduces the likelihood of collective resistance to capitalism. 1 mark for a further development: e.g. Zaretsky argued the family also acts as a unit of consumption, purchasing goods that generate profit for the bourgeoisie, and performs an ideological function by making capitalist social relations appear natural.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the family benefits all its members equally.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both sides of the debate developed with named sociologists, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a supported judgement. For (the family benefits all): Parsons's functionalist argument that the two irreducible functions (primary socialisation and personality stabilisation) benefit children, adults and society as a whole; the warm bath theory suggests both partners gain emotional stability. Against: Feminist view (Oakley; Delphy and Leonard) that the family primarily benefits men through women's unpaid labour; the double shift and triple shift show women bear disproportionate burdens; Marxist view (Zaretsky) that the family benefits the bourgeoisie rather than workers. New Right (Murray) argues traditional family benefits all, but implies some family forms are more beneficial than others. Supported conclusion that weighs which perspective is most convincing.

Secure: Both sides present, at least one named sociologist, judgement at the end.

Developing: Relevant points, mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the conflict versus consensus debate about the role of the family in society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a clear supported judgement. Consensus (functionalist): Parsons's primary socialisation and warm bath theory; instrumental and expressive roles as complementary; the New Right's endorsement of the traditional nuclear family. Conflict perspectives: Marxist (Zaretsky) — the family serves capitalism, not society; reproduces the workforce, absorbs discontent, unit of consumption, ideological function; feminist (Delphy and Leonard) — the family is a patriarchal economic institution exploiting women's labour; Oakley's conventional family and double shift. Comparison of consensus and conflict claims: both identify 'functions' but disagree on who benefits. Sociological vocabulary (primary socialisation, instrumental role, patriarchy, bourgeoisie, ideological function, underclass, dependency culture) used accurately. Comparison and contrast of perspectives explicit. Substantiated conclusion that weighs the evidence.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes Merton's concept of 'innovation' as a response to strain?
A) Accepting both the cultural goals and the legitimate means of achieving them
B) Abandoning both cultural goals and the means of achieving them
C) Accepting cultural goals but using deviant or criminal means to achieve them
D) Rejecting cultural goals but continuing to follow the rules rigidly
practice_questions.marks: C) Accepting cultural goals but using deviant or criminal means to achieve them [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what sociologists mean by the term 'anomie'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying anomie as a state of normlessness or the breakdown of social rules/norms. 1 mark for extending this with context: e.g. Durkheim introduced the term to describe what happens when the rules that regulate individual desires break down, leaving people without clear moral guidance; Merton developed it to describe the strain caused when cultural goals outweigh the legitimate means of achieving them. Either developmental point earns the second mark.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one of Merton's five responses to strain, other than conformity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming one of: Innovation, Ritualism, Retreatism, Rebellion. 2 marks for a developed description that explains the combination of goals and means involved. Example: Innovation (1) — the individual accepts the cultural goal of material success but either lacks access to or rejects the legitimate means of achieving it, turning instead to criminal methods such as theft or fraud (2).

practice_questions.text: Describe Albert Cohen's subcultural theory of crime, including the concept of status frustration.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying Cohen's focus on working-class boys and their shared mainstream success goals. 1 mark for explaining that cultural deprivation and educational failure mean these goals cannot be achieved through legitimate means. 1 mark for explaining status frustration: the resentment and frustration that results from this failure. 1 mark for explaining how delinquent sub-cultures form as a collective response, inverting mainstream values so that deviant acts (vandalism, truancy, theft) earn prestige within the group via an alternative status hierarchy.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that functionalist theories best explain why crime is found in every society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides addressed with named sociologists and sociological vocabulary, reaching a supported judgement. In support: Durkheim's argument that a certain level of crime is normal and functional in all societies (boundary maintenance, social change); Merton's strain theory showing crime as a structural response to cultural goals and blocked opportunities; these theories have broad cross-cultural application and focus on social structure rather than individual pathology. Against or qualifying: Marxist critique that functionalism ignores the class bias in law enforcement; feminist critique that Merton and Durkheim both largely ignore women; interactionist critique that functionalism assumes a shared value consensus that does not account for subcultural diversity; Cohen extends functionalism but is limited to young working-class males. Student names at least Durkheim and Merton alongside one contrasting perspective, presents both sides and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: both sides covered with named theorists, judgement present. Developing: one-sided or underdeveloped. Emerging: basic descriptive points, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that crime is caused by the way society is structured, not by the choices of individuals.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. For the claim: Merton's strain theory (crime as a structural response to the goals-means gap; innovation most common among those denied legitimate routes to success); Cohen's subcultural theory (status frustration produced by class structure and educational failure); Marxist view that the structure of capitalism itself generates crime by producing inequality. Against or qualifying: Interactionist perspective (Becker) argues that individual labelling processes, not structure alone, determine who becomes criminal; feminist perspective points out that structural theories largely ignore women's experiences of crime and control; New Right perspective (Murray) argues that individual choices and a dependency culture, not structural barriers, explain crime patterns. Student names at least two contrasting theorists and develops their arguments. Reaches a supported judgement that weighs the evidence on both sides. Secure: both structural and non-structural arguments covered, named sociologists present, judgement reached. Developing: mostly one-sided or limited development, some theorists named. Emerging: descriptive, few named theorists, little evaluative judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of data is expressed in numerical form and can be analysed statistically?
A) Qualitative data
B) Secondary data
C) Quantitative data
D) Primary data
practice_questions.marks: C) Quantitative data [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'triangulation' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating it involves using more than one method or data source; 1 mark for indicating the purpose is to cross-check findings and compensate for the weaknesses of individual methods, increasing confidence in the conclusions. Example: 'Triangulation involves using two or more research methods or data sources in the same study so that the weaknesses of one approach are compensated for by the strengths of another.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one advantage of using unstructured interviews and describe why this makes them suitable for studying sensitive social topics.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage of unstructured interviews (e.g. generates rich qualitative data, allows participants to raise unexpected themes, builds rapport, follows the participant's own framework of meaning). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying that unstructured interviews build rapport (1 mark) and explaining that for sensitive topics such as domestic abuse or experiences of discrimination, the conversational and non-directive format allows participants to feel more comfortable sharing personal experiences; the interviewer can adjust tone and pacing in response to emotional cues, producing more honest and valid data than a standardised questionnaire (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the strengths and weaknesses of questionnaires as a method of sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for strengths: questionnaires can reach a large sample quickly and at low cost; responses are standardised so data can be compared statistically; anonymity may increase honest responses on sensitive topics; the study can be replicated, improving reliability. Up to 2 marks for weaknesses: response rates may be low and non-respondents may differ from respondents, introducing bias; closed questions impose the researcher's categories on complex experiences; questionnaires cannot probe unexpected answers; respondents from different social groups may interpret the same question differently, reducing validity.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that official statistics are a more valuable source of data for sociologists than qualitative methods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments supporting official statistics: large-scale, nationally consistent, free to access, allow long-term trend analysis; the Crime Survey for England and Wales interviews about 31,000 adults a year and picks up crimes never reported to the police. Arguments against: official statistics are limited by under-reporting (the dark figure of unrecorded crime); they are politically produced and may reflect government priorities rather than social reality; different perspectives interpret the same statistics differently (functionalist, Marxist and interactionist readings diverge). Qualitative methods (participant observation, unstructured interviews) may offer insight statistics obscure. The answer names at least two perspectives or contexts, uses sociological vocabulary (validity, reliability, dark figure), and reaches a supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one named perspective or method cited; a judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some concepts named; conclusion present but assertive.

Emerging: Basic description of statistics or methods; little evaluation; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that participant observation is the most valuable method available to sociologists studying social groups.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour: participant observation produces highly valid data that captures real behaviour in natural settings; Willis (1977, Learning to Labour) reveals depth of counter-school culture not accessible by questionnaire; interactionists value it for accessing the subjective meanings of participants. Arguments against: raises serious ethical concerns (covert observation violates informed consent; participant safety may be compromised in dangerous settings); researcher may 'go native'; extremely time-consuming; findings are not generalisable beyond the specific group; positivist researchers argue it lacks reliability because it cannot be replicated. The answer evaluates practical, ethical and theoretical dimensions, cites at least two named perspectives or studies, and reaches a clear supported judgement about when and for whom participant observation is most valuable.

Secure: Arguments for and against addressed; at least one named study or perspective; a judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive; some evaluation but undeveloped; conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of participant observation; little evaluation; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes an 'empty shell marriage'?
A) A marriage that has been legally ended through divorce
B) A marriage that continues legally but in which the emotional relationship between partners has effectively ended
C) A marriage in which both partners work full-time and rarely see each other
D) A marriage involving two partners who have no children
practice_questions.marks: B) A marriage that continues legally but in which the emotional relationship between partners has effectively ended [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'domestic violence' as understood in GCSE Sociology.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it involves harm or abuse between intimate partners or family members; 1 mark for specifying that it includes physical violence, controlling behaviour, coercive control, psychological harm or economic abuse. Example: 'Domestic violence refers to abuse occurring between intimate partners or family members, including physical violence, psychological harm, controlling behaviour and coercive control, predominantly affecting women.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one criticism of the view that the family is always a safe and supportive environment.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant criticism (e.g. domestic violence; social isolation; idealisation of family life concealing abuse; the dark side of family life). 2 marks for a developed description with a sociological perspective or named sociologist: e.g. 'Feminist sociologists argue that domestic violence is a structural consequence of patriarchy within the family. The Crime Survey for England and Wales data shows around 2.1 million adults experienced domestic abuse in a single year, with the majority of victims being women. Feminist sociologists such as Oakley argue this is not an individual aberration but evidence that the family as currently structured concentrates male authority in a private space, systematically disadvantaging women.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the isolation critique of the modern nuclear family.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying isolation as a criticism (the nuclear family has become cut off from wider kinship and community networks). 1 mark for describing the mechanism: as nuclear families became more privatised and home-centred, they lost the external support of extended kinship networks. 1 mark for a consequence: this places intense pressure on individual family members during times of crisis, as there is no wider network to share the burden. 1 mark for a developed point or sociological link: critics argue that isolated nuclear families are more vulnerable to conflict, domestic abuse and mental health problems — the opposite of the warm bath effect Parsons described. The privatised nature of the family makes these problems harder to identify and address.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the family is harmful to its members.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both sides of the argument presented with named sociologists and perspectives, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a supported judgement. For (harmful): feminist view (Oakley) — the family exploits women through unpaid domestic labour; domestic violence as a structural consequence of patriarchy; isolation and idealisation concealing abuse; empty shell marriages. Against (not harmful): functionalist response (Parsons, Murdock) — dysfunctional families are failures of the institution, not evidence against it; the family still performs irreplaceable primary socialisation; the warm bath of emotional support is a genuine benefit for most families. New Right (Murray) — the problem is family diversity, not the family per se. Supported conclusion that weighs the evidence on both sides.

Secure: Both sides present, at least one named sociologist, judgement at the end.

Developing: Relevant points, mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that domestic violence demonstrates the family is a fundamentally patriarchal institution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a clear supported judgement. For (family as patriarchal): feminist argument (Oakley) — domestic violence is a structural consequence of patriarchal power relations concentrated in a private space; Crime Survey for England and Wales data (2.1 million victims annually, majority women) supports the scale of the problem; women's role within the family is constructed around unpaid domestic service; the double shift shows that even as women gained paid employment, family inequality persisted. Against or qualification: not all families involve domestic violence; functionalists (Parsons) argue the warm bath theory holds for most families; the New Right argues family diversity (lone parent households) rather than the nuclear family itself is the source of problems; legal reforms and greater social awareness have reduced domestic violence in many contexts. Sociological vocabulary (patriarchy, domestic violence, conventional family, isolation, idealisation, empty shell marriage) used accurately. Comparison and contrast of perspectives explicit. Substantiated conclusion.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist revisited the Luton car-plant workers in the early 1990s to study class identity and life chances?
A) Goldthorpe
B) Townsend
C) Walby
D) Devine
practice_questions.marks: D) Devine [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'life chances'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that life chances refer to the opportunities available to an individual to improve their quality of life; 1 mark for linking this to social position or structural factors. Example: 'Life chances are the opportunities an individual has to improve their quality of life, such as access to education, health and employment, which are shaped by their position in the social structure including their class, gender and ethnicity.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way that gender affects life chances in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying one way gender affects life chances (e.g. the gender pay gap; over-representation of women in low-paid part-time work; the glass ceiling; women's greater likelihood of poverty in old age). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Women in the UK earn less on average than men in comparable occupations, a pattern described as the gender pay gap. This affects their overall financial security, pension accumulation and economic independence over the life course. Feminist sociologists link this to patriarchal structures that undervalue women's labour and create barriers to senior positions — the glass ceiling — rather than to differences in ability or effort.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Devine's key findings from her study of affluent workers.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Devine revisited Luton in the late 1980s, interviewing manual workers and their partners at the same site as Goldthorpe and Lockwood's original 1960s study (1 mark). She did not find evidence to support embourgeoisement — workers had not absorbed middle-class values or abandoned class identity (1 mark). Workers retained a strong sense of class identity and resentment at extreme inequality despite rising living standards and consumer aspirations (1 mark). Many had also lost faith in the Labour Party as a vehicle for change, but had not abandoned their awareness of structural inequality (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that social mobility means inequality in life chances is decreasing in modern Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides, sustained vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: evidence of upward social mobility; educational expansion means more working-class students reaching university; functionalist view that meritocracy is operating. Contrasting: Marxist view that structural barriers mean mobility is limited and class inequality in life chances is reproduced across generations; Devine's finding that class identity persists even among affluent workers; private schooling and social closure as mechanisms reproducing elite advantage; evidence of persistent gender pay gap, disability employment gap, ethnic inequality. Named sociologists and precise vocabulary throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement offered.

Developing: Mostly one-sided; some vocabulary; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description; few named sociologists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that social class is the most important factor shaping life chances in contemporary Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Class as a factor argued in depth: material deprivation, private schooling and social closure, cultural capital, Devine's evidence that class identity and awareness of inequality persist; Marxist structural reproduction. At least two other factors developed as serious alternatives: gender (feminist perspective, Walby on patriarchy, glass ceiling, gender pay gap — affects women across all class positions); ethnicity (institutional racism, employment discrimination, structural inequality beyond individual prejudice). Functionalist counter-argument acknowledged: differential life chances may reflect meritocratic rewards for different levels of talent and effort. Evidence weighed: class remains a strong predictor but intersects with other factors. Supported judgement about whether class is the most important single factor or whether intersecting dimensions offer a more complete account.

Secure: Most arguments present; multiple factors developed; judgement offered.

Developing: Class discussed but limited treatment of other factors; weak evaluation; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of class inequality; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best summarises the finding of Chambliss's Saints and Roughnecks study?
A) Working-class boys committed more crime than middle-class boys in the study
B) Middle-class boys were arrested more often because they were more visible to the police
C) Despite similar levels of offending, working-class boys were consistently arrested while middle-class boys were not
D) The study found no significant difference in how police treated the two groups
practice_questions.marks: C) Despite similar levels of offending, working-class boys were consistently arrested while middle-class boys were not [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'differential enforcement of the law'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that the law is applied unequally across social groups. 1 mark for specifying the basis of the inequality: working-class individuals are more likely to be stopped, arrested and prosecuted than middle- or upper-class individuals committing similar acts; the enforcement reflects social characteristics rather than solely the nature of the offence. Example: 'Differential enforcement of the law refers to the unequal application of criminal law, in which working-class individuals are more likely to be targeted by police and prosecution than middle-class individuals committing equivalent acts.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe how a deviant career may develop following the application of a criminal label.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the deviant career as the process by which a labelled individual is progressively drawn into a deviant identity. 2 marks for a developed description: the labelled person is excluded from legitimate opportunities (employment, housing, education) because the master status precedes them; this makes conventional life harder, producing a self-fulfilling prophecy; the individual increasingly identifies with the label and joins organised deviant groups, completing what Becker called the deviant career.

practice_questions.text: Describe Heidensohn's feminist explanation for women's lower rates of criminal behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying Heidensohn's argument that women face more intensive patriarchal control than men, making it harder to deviate. 1 mark for describing control in the home: domestic expectations, male violence as an assertion of authority, financial dependence on male breadwinners. 1 mark for control in public: threat of male sexual violence, separate spheres ideology limiting independent movement. 1 mark for control at work: male-dominated hierarchies, sexual harassment and limited organisational power. Or: 2 marks for two well-developed domains of control with clear explanation of how each restricts women's opportunities to offend.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that it is the reaction of others, not the act itself, that makes someone a criminal.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides addressed with named sociologists and sociological vocabulary, reaching a supported judgement. In support: interactionist evidence (Becker, Outsiders 1963) that the same act receives different labels depending on who commits it and who observes; Chambliss (Saints and Roughnecks 1973) showing class-based differential enforcement; crime statistics reflect policing practices as much as actual offending. Against or qualifying: Merton's strain theory argues that structural conditions, not reactions alone, cause crime; functionalists argue some acts are universally condemned regardless of who commits them; Marxist critique that labelling theory describes but does not explain why labels fall on the working class without reference to class power. Student names at least Becker plus one contrasting perspective and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: both sides covered with named theorists, judgement present. Developing: mostly one perspective with limited evaluation. Emerging: basic descriptions, few theorists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations for why women commit fewer crimes than men.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. Relevant explanations: Heidensohn (Women and Crime, 1985) — patriarchal control in home, public and work restricts women's opportunities; Carlen (Women, Crime and Poverty, 1988) — class and gender deals break down for some women, making crime a rational choice; functionalist gender socialisation — boys socialised to be aggressive and risk-taking, girls to be conformist; chivalry thesis — criminal justice system treats women more leniently when they conform to feminine stereotypes. Critiques: Heidensohn's account does not explain all women equally (varies by class, ethnicity, age); Carlen's small sample limits generalisation; female offending rates have changed since 1985; the chivalry thesis is contested (women who deviate from gender norms may face harsher treatment). Student names at least Heidensohn and Carlen, presents multiple perspectives, weighs the evidence and reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: most arguments present, both sides covered, judgement reached. Developing: relevant points but mostly one-sided or underdeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which sampling method involves initial participants recruiting others from their social networks and is best suited to studying hard-to-reach populations?
A) Stratified sample
B) Systematic sample
C) Quota sample
D) Snowball sample
practice_questions.marks: D) Snowball sample [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'informed consent' as used in sociological research ethics.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating consent requires participants to agree to take part; 1 mark for indicating they must be given full, honest information about the study and must agree voluntarily, with the right to withdraw. Example: 'Informed consent means that participants must be given clear and honest information about the study and must voluntarily agree to take part before data collection begins.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one practical issue that sociologists face when conducting research and describe how it can affect the quality of data collected.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a practical issue (time, cost or access). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying access (1 mark) and explaining that if a gatekeeper (such as a school head teacher) restricts access to certain participants — for example, excluding students with poor behaviour records from a study of school exclusion — the resulting sample will be biased and unrepresentative, meaning findings cannot be generalised and the validity of the research is undermined (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two ethical issues a sociologist might face when conducting research with vulnerable participants, and explain how each can be addressed.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for the first ethical issue: e.g. harm to participants — discussing traumatic experiences may cause psychological distress; the researcher can address this by offering a debrief session, providing signposting to relevant support services, and stopping the research if the participant shows signs of distress (1 mark for identifying harm, 1 mark for a practical solution). Up to 2 marks for the second issue: e.g. informed consent with children — children cannot legally give consent themselves; the researcher must obtain written consent from a parent or guardian and age-appropriate assent from the child, explaining the study in accessible language (1 mark for identifying the consent challenge, 1 mark for the practical solution).

practice_questions.text: Identify one ethical problem created by using covert observation as a research method and describe how a researcher might attempt to address it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an ethical problem specific to covert observation (e.g. deception violates informed consent; participants cannot withdraw because they do not know they are being studied; the researcher may observe illegal activity and face a legal or moral dilemma). Up to 2 marks for a developed description of how it might be addressed. Example: identifying deception (1 mark) and explaining that some researchers address this by conducting a full debrief as soon as the covert phase is complete, informing participants of the research, offering the right to withdraw data, and seeking retrospective consent — though critics argue this does not fully resolve the original deception (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that ethical guidelines make some of the most valuable sociological research impossible to conduct.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for both sides. Arguments in favour: some research questions (gang violence, covert institutional racism, hidden drug networks) genuinely cannot be investigated through fully consented transparent methods; the Hawthorne effect means fully transparent research produces less valid data on sensitive behaviour; historically important covert research has shaped policy in ways that fully consented research could not. Arguments against: ethical guidelines protect vulnerable participants from exploitation; the BSA guidelines provide practical solutions (anonymisation, debriefs, ethics committees) that allow sensitive research to proceed; research violating ethical principles lacks academic credibility; feminist researchers argue participant-centred approaches produce richer and more valid data than covert extraction. At least two perspectives or named methods cited. A clear supported judgement about where the balance lies.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one named method or context; a judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive; some relevant points; conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of ethical issues; little evaluative engagement; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a free school?
A) A state school that charges no fees because state education is free
B) A state-funded school set up by parents, charities or other groups outside local authority control
C) A school that selects pupils on academic ability via the eleven-plus
D) A school funded by a religious organisation with selective admissions
practice_questions.marks: B) A state-funded school set up by parents, charities or other groups outside local authority control [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'marketisation of education'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the application of market principles to education; 1 mark for explaining what this means in practice. Example: 'Marketisation of education is the process by which market principles — competition between schools for pupils, parental choice and performance measures such as league tables — are applied to the organisation of schooling, on the assumption that competition drives up standards.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one sociological argument against grammar schools.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid argument (e.g. grammar schools entrench class inequality / middle-class families can afford eleven-plus tutoring / working-class pupils are disproportionately excluded); 2 marks for a developed description naming the mechanism. Example: 'Critics of grammar schools argue that they entrench class inequality because middle-class families have the resources to pay for private tuition to prepare their children for the eleven-plus examination, while working-class families typically cannot. The result is that grammar schools disproportionately serve middle-class pupils rather than the academically talented from all backgrounds that their supporters claim they serve.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Ball's argument about how marketisation of education reinforces social class inequality.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Point 1: Ball argued that middle-class parents use their cultural capital to navigate the competitive school market: they read and interpret league tables, visit multiple schools, write effective appeals and use social networks to access information. Working-class parents care equally but lack the same information and resources, making 'parental choice' less meaningful in practice. Point 2: Middle-class families can also move into the catchment areas of high-performing schools — a strategy requiring both economic resources and the cultural knowledge of which schools are worth pursuing. Ball's conclusion is that market competition reinforces existing class inequalities rather than levelling the playing field, concentrating advantage among families already most privileged.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that having different types of school benefits all pupils in society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Arguments for: functionalists argue school diversity allows meritocratic role allocation (grammar schools channel academic pupils, vocational routes others); New Right argues competition drives up standards for all schools. Arguments against: Marxists argue private schools allow the bourgeoisie to purchase educational advantage, passing privilege across generations rather than allocating it on merit; Ball's research shows marketisation advantages middle-class families; grammar schools disproportionately serve middle-class pupils who can afford eleven-plus tutoring. Feminist perspective: historically school types were designed around male education; comprehensive co-education improved gender equality, but some faith schools may reinforce gendered expectations. At least two perspectives with named sociologists. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Supported judgement. Secure (5-7): Both sides, named sociologists, judgement present. Developing (3-4): Mostly one-sided, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-2): Basic description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that private schools are the main cause of educational inequality in contemporary Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of arguments for and against. Arguments for: private schools concentrate educational advantage for the wealthy; approximately 7% of pupils but a disproportionate share of elite professionals; Marxist argument that the bourgeoisie purchases intergenerational privilege through fee-paying schools. Arguments against or complicating: class inequality also operates within the state sector (Ball on marketisation, Halsey on class barriers even with comprehensive schooling); grammar schools within the state sector also create selection-based inequality accessible to those who can afford tutoring; other factors such as material deprivation and cultural capital produce inequality regardless of private schooling. A judgement that weighs whether private schools are the main cause or one factor among several. Comparison of perspectives explicit. Secure (7-9): Most arguments present, named sociologists, clear judgement. Developing (4-6): One-sided or undeveloped, some named theorists, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic description, few named sociologists, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'relative poverty'?
A) Lacking enough food to survive physically
B) Earning less than the national average wage
C) Lacking resources to participate in the standard of living considered normal in society
D) Having no access to state welfare benefits
practice_questions.marks: C) Lacking resources to participate in the standard of living considered normal in society [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'absolute poverty'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that absolute poverty refers to a lack of basic necessities; 1 mark for specifying what those necessities are or explaining that the threshold is fixed (e.g. 'Absolute poverty is a condition in which an individual lacks the minimum resources required for physical survival, such as adequate food, shelter and clothing, measured against a fixed threshold that does not vary with overall living standards in society.').

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the concept of the 'cycle of deprivation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the cycle of deprivation as the intergenerational reproduction of poverty. 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'The cycle of deprivation describes how poverty can be self-reinforcing across generations. Children raised in poverty face interconnected disadvantages — in nutrition, housing quality, educational resources and aspirations — that reduce their chances of escaping poverty as adults. Limited educational attainment restricts employment prospects; limited income creates material deprivation for the next generation. Structural interventions at the level of income, housing and education are therefore needed to break the cycle, rather than focusing on individual behaviour.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Murray's New Right explanation of poverty, including the concept of the underclass.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Murray argued that welfare benefits created a growing underclass dependent on state support rather than employment (1 mark); he identified a dependency culture — a set of values normalising benefit receipt and undermining work and family responsibility (1 mark); he identified rising lone parenthood, crime and youth unemployment as signs of underclass growth (1 mark); critics argue Murray's evidence is weak, that most benefit recipients hold conventional values and aspire to employment, and that his analysis ignores structural causes including the gender pay gap and globalisation (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that poverty in modern Britain is best explained by the behaviour and attitudes of poor people themselves.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides, sustained vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: Murray's New Right underclass and dependency culture thesis explained in depth — welfare dependency, rising lone parenthood, unwillingness to seek employment. Contrasting: Townsend's structural relative deprivation approach (poverty as lack of resources for social participation, deprivation index, 22%); Marxist explanation (structural class exploitation, globalisation increasing labour insecurity); feminist critique of Murray (victim-blames lone mothers, ignores gender pay gap and domestic responsibilities). Named sociologists throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both cultural and structural sides present; named sociologists; judgement offered.

Developing: Mostly one side; some vocabulary; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations of poverty in contemporary British society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Cultural explanation (Murray's underclass, dependency culture) explained and evaluated with evidence against it. Structural explanations developed in depth: Townsend's relative deprivation and deprivation index (22% finding, social participation measure); Marxist explanation (class exploitation, surplus value extraction, globalisation relocating manufacturing and increasing insecurity); feminist critique (poverty disproportionately affects women — lone parents, elderly women on low pensions — linked to gender pay gap and domestic responsibilities — Walby's structures of patriarchy). Cycle of deprivation and social exclusion as structural frameworks. Groups prone to poverty identified (lone parents, elderly, ethnic minorities). Supported judgement weighing cultural versus structural explanations, noting the evidence strongly supports structural accounts.

Secure: Most arguments present; Townsend and Murray both developed; contrasting perspectives used; judgement offered.

Developing: Mostly Townsend or Murray without sufficient evaluation of the other; weak comparative structure; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of poverty types; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which source of crime data asks members of the public about crimes they have experienced as victims, whether or not they reported them to the police?
A) Police-recorded crime statistics
B) The Crime Survey for England and Wales
C) Court conviction records
D) Prison population data
practice_questions.marks: B) The Crime Survey for England and Wales [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'the dark figure of crime'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that it refers to crime that does not appear in official statistics. 1 mark for specifying that this is because crimes are not reported to the police or not recorded by them. Example: 'The dark figure of crime is the gap between the amount of crime that actually occurs and the amount officially recorded, caused by victims not reporting incidents and by the police not recording all reported crimes.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one reason why a victim of domestic violence might not report the crime to the police.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant reason (e.g. fear of the perpetrator; financial dependence; shame; distrust of police response; not recognising the behaviour as criminal). 2 marks for a developed description with sociological reasoning. Example: 'Victims of domestic violence may not report the crime because they fear or are financially dependent on the perpetrator (1). Feminist sociologists argue that patriarchal norms also discourage women from reporting sexual and domestic violence because of shame and the fear of victim-blaming responses from police and courts, resulting in a particularly large dark figure for these offences (2 marks for a developed sociological point).'

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Crime Survey for England and Wales differs from police-recorded crime as a source of data.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Likely content: The CSEW is a large-scale victim survey that asks households directly about crimes they have experienced (1), whereas police-recorded crime is based on incidents reported to and recorded by the police (1). The CSEW captures many crimes that are never reported to the police, producing higher estimates of crime levels (1). Because the CSEW is independent of policing decisions, it is less affected by changes in recording practices, making it a more consistent basis for long-term trend analysis (1).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that invisible crime reveals important limitations in official crime statistics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides addressed with named sociologists and sociological vocabulary, reaching a supported judgement. In support: domestic abuse is systematically absent from official statistics because victims fear or depend on perpetrators; environmental and white-collar crime lacks obvious victims who report to police; Marxist argument that the concept of invisible crime shows how official statistics protect the powerful while overrepresenting the visible poor; feminist argument that crimes against women have a particularly large dark figure. Against or qualifying: official statistics do capture serious violence and property crime reliably; the CSEW provides some measure of domestic violence; invisible crime is not a single category and some forms are increasingly recorded. Student names at least one perspective, presents both sides and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: both sides covered, some named perspectives, judgement present. Developing: one-sided or underdeveloped, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic descriptive points, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of official crime statistics as a source of data for sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. For the usefulness: official statistics are large-scale, nationally consistent, allow long-term trend analysis and cover the entire population; functionalist perspective accepts them as broadly useful for monitoring social order; police-recorded crime offers the longest historical run of data. Against the usefulness: the dark figure means official statistics systematically under-represent crime; Marxist critique that law and policing priorities protect ruling-class interests, concealing corporate and white-collar crime while inflating working-class crime; feminist critique that crimes against women (domestic violence, sexual assault) have a particularly large dark figure due to patriarchal norms and inadequate police response; interactionist argument that statistics measure policing activity rather than actual offending (self-report studies show offending more evenly spread). Invisible crime (domestic abuse, environmental offences) further demonstrates systematic exclusion from official data. A clear, supported judgement weighing these critiques. Secure: most arguments, both sides, named perspectives, judgement present. Developing: mostly one-sided or underdeveloped. Emerging: basic descriptive points, little sociological reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which piece of legislation in 1969, in force from 1971, made divorce substantially easier to obtain in England and Wales by introducing 'irretrievable breakdown of marriage' as grounds for divorce?
A) The Family Law Act 1965
B) The Marriage Act 1960
C) The Divorce Reform Act 1969
D) The Matrimonial Causes Act 1950
practice_questions.marks: C) The Divorce Reform Act 1969 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'serial monogamy'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it involves a series of relationships or marriages; 1 mark for specifying these are monogamous (one at a time rather than simultaneously). Example: 'Serial monogamy is the practice of having a series of monogamous relationships or marriages in sequence rather than simultaneously, which has become more common as divorce and remarriage rates have both risen.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one consequence of divorce for the extended family.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a consequence for the extended family (e.g. grandparents on the non-resident parent's side may lose contact with grandchildren; disruption of wider kinship networks). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'When a couple with children divorces and the children remain with one parent, grandparents on the non-resident parent's side may lose regular contact with their grandchildren, as they no longer see them through the resident parent's household. This can disrupt long-standing grandparent-grandchild relationships and sever important intergenerational bonds, contributing to the isolation of elderly family members as well as reducing support networks for the children themselves.'

practice_questions.text: Describe how secularisation has contributed to rising divorce rates in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying secularisation as the long-term decline in the social influence of religion. 1 mark for explaining the link to divorce: the Church of England and Roman Catholic Church traditionally taught marriage was a lifelong sacrament and that divorce was morally wrong. 1 mark for the mechanism: as church attendance fell and religious authority over personal life weakened, the stigma attached to divorce diminished, making it more socially acceptable. 1 mark for a further development: by the end of the twentieth century divorce carried little social stigma in most communities, and what had previously been a morally charged decision became largely a personal and legal one.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that rising divorce rates in the UK are primarily caused by changes in women's status in society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both sides of the debate developed with named sociologists, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a supported judgement. For women's changing status as primary cause: women's entry into paid employment gave greater economic independence, reducing financial dependence on marriage; majority of divorce petitions filed by women; Oakley's double shift means women experience marriage as disproportionately burdensome; rising expectations of gender equality made inequality in marriage less tolerable. Against (or qualification): legal change (Divorce Reform Act 1969 and 2022 no-fault reform) is equally or more significant as a proximate cause; secularisation removed religious stigma independently of women's status; economic pressures (Marxist view, Zaretsky) also play a role. Named sociologists (Oakley, Parsons, Murray) developed in detail. Supported conclusion.

Secure: Both sides present, at least one named sociologist, judgement at the end.

Developing: Relevant points, mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that rising divorce rates show the family as an institution is in decline in modern Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a clear supported judgement. For (family in decline): New Right (Murray) — rising divorce and lone parenthood contribute to an underclass, poverty and educational underachievement; high divorce rates suggest marriages are failing; children disadvantaged by family breakdown. Against (not in decline): Functionalist view (Parsons) — the family adapts to meet changing social needs; high remarriage rates show the institution of marriage is still valued (serial monogamy); the Divorce Reform Act 1969 and 2022 no-fault reform made legal divorce easier, so rising rates partly reflect legal change rather than relationship failure. Feminist view — rising rates reflect women's growing independence, representing progress not crisis. Marxist view (Zaretsky) — marital breakdown driven by economic pressures of capitalism, not family values; the family persists as a unit serving capitalism. Empty shell marriages show official divorce statistics undercount breakdown. Sociological vocabulary (secularisation, serial monogamy, empty shell marriage, dependency culture, lone parent family, no-fault divorce) used accurately. Comparison and contrast of perspectives explicit. Substantiated conclusion.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which research method did Willis use in his 1977 study 'Learning to Labour'?
A) Structured questionnaire
B) Analysis of official statistics
C) Participant observation
D) Structured interviews only
practice_questions.marks: C) Participant observation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'triangulation' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that triangulation involves using more than one research method; 1 mark for explaining that the purpose is to cross-check or compare findings to increase confidence in conclusions. Example: 'Triangulation is the use of more than one research method in a single study, so that findings from one method can be checked against findings from another, increasing confidence in the conclusions. For example, Ball combined classroom observation with interviews in his Beachside Comprehensive research.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one practical problem sociologists face when conducting research in schools.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid practical issue (access through gatekeepers / researcher influence / time and cost / obtaining parental consent); 2 marks for a developed description applying the issue specifically to educational research. Example: 'Gaining access to schools requires permission from several gatekeepers — the headteacher must agree to the research, individual teachers must open their classrooms, and parents must give consent for their children to participate. Each level of gatekeeping can distort the data: a headteacher might only allow observation of their best lessons, meaning the researcher never sees everyday school life. This limits the validity of the findings.'

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of using official statistics to research educational achievement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Strength: official statistics from the Department for Education are large-scale, covering all state schools in England, and longitudinal — allowing researchers to track attainment trends by class, gender and ethnicity over many years, as Halsey did in Origins and Destinations. This gives high reliability: the same data can be cross-checked and compared by different researchers. Weakness: official statistics are socially constructed — they reflect decisions about what to measure. League tables measure exam results but not the value a school adds to pupils' progress. A school serving a disadvantaged intake may appear less effective than one in a wealthy catchment area, when in reality it may be adding more to its pupils' development.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that participant observation is the best method for researching what happens inside schools.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Arguments for: participant observation generates high validity — Willis's Learning to Labour is the classic example, revealing counter-school culture through months of direct observation. Arguments against: practical problems — access requires multiple gatekeepers; researcher influence changes classroom behaviour (reducing validity); time-consuming and expensive; findings may lack generalisability (Willis studied twelve boys in one school). Alternative methods: official statistics allow large-scale trend analysis (Halsey); interviews allow focused exploration of specific issues; triangulation (Ball) combines both. A judgement that weighs whether participant observation is 'best' in context or whether the most appropriate method depends on the research question. Named sociologists from the education unit used as examples. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Secure (5-7): Both sides, named examples, judgement present. Developing (3-4): Mostly one-sided, some examples, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-2): Basic description of one method, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the ethical issues sociologists face when researching the experiences of pupils in schools.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of ethical issues addressed with specific strategies. Informed consent: complex with children because parental consent is also required; this may introduce class bias (only engaged parents respond). Strategy: written consent forms sent home, clear explanation of research aims, right to withdraw stated. Confidentiality: pupils may share sensitive information about labelling, poverty or bullying. Strategy: pseudonyms for schools and individuals (Willis: Hammertown; Ball: Beachside), anonymisation in publications. Harm to participants: sensitive questions about negative school experiences can cause psychological distress. Strategy: sensitive interviewing, debriefing, withdrawal rights. Tension between confidentiality and safeguarding: if a researcher discovers serious harm, the duty to report overrides confidentiality. Judgement that weighs whether ethical issues in school research can be fully resolved or whether they involve ongoing tensions. Comparison and contrast of strategies is explicit. Secure (7-9): All three ethical issues addressed with strategies, judgement present. Developing (4-6): One or two issues described with strategies, one-sided, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic list of issues, no strategies, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which stage of the research design process involves defining abstract concepts (such as 'social class') in a way that can be measured or observed?
A) Sampling
B) Hypothesis formation
C) Operationalisation
D) Triangulation
practice_questions.marks: C) Operationalisation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'hypothesis' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating a hypothesis is a prediction or statement to be tested; 1 mark for indicating it predicts a relationship between variables and can be supported or refuted by evidence. Example: 'A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about a relationship between two or more variables, stated before data collection and either supported or refuted by the findings.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one advantage of conducting a pilot study and describe how it would improve the quality of a sociological investigation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. identifies ambiguous questions, reveals whether the sampling method is practical, tests the consent process, indicates how long the study will take). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying that a pilot study identifies ambiguous questions (1 mark) and explaining that if a question is interpreted differently by different respondents, the resulting data cannot be meaningfully compared; revising the question after the pilot ensures all participants understand it the same way, improving the reliability and validity of the main data (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a research aim and a hypothesis, and explain why operationalisation is an important stage in research design.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for distinguishing aim and hypothesis: a research aim is a broad statement of purpose (what the study sets out to investigate); a hypothesis is a more specific, testable prediction about the relationship between two variables that the research will seek to support or refute. Up to 2 marks for explaining operationalisation: abstract concepts such as 'poverty' or 'social class' must be given precise, measurable definitions before data can be collected; different operationalisations produce different findings, so the researcher must make their definition explicit for the research to be evaluated and replicated.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that being able to interpret data is as important a skill for sociology students as knowing sociological theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments supporting data interpretation as equally important: GCSE Sociology requires students to describe patterns from charts and tables before explaining them; without accurate description, sociological explanation rests on false premises; the specification explicitly demands data-interpretation skills as a separate strand. Arguments that theory is more important: raw data is meaningless without theoretical frameworks to interpret it; the same statistics can be read in opposite ways by functionalists, Marxists and interactionists; sociological research questions are themselves theory-driven. The answer uses sociological vocabulary (quantitative/qualitative data, patterns, trends, official statistics), names at least one perspective or context, and reaches a clear supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides addressed; at least one relevant concept or context cited; a judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some sociological language used; conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points about data or theory; little balance; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics as a source of data when investigating patterns of educational attainment in the United Kingdom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of arguments for both sides. Strengths: official statistics on attainment (e.g. from the Department for Education) cover all state schools in England, are nationally consistent, allow long-term trend analysis, and enable comparison by class (free school meals eligibility), gender and ethnicity. Limitations: official statistics may reflect how categories are constructed rather than underlying reality (e.g. free school meals eligibility as a proxy for class is imprecise); they do not capture private school data comprehensively; they show patterns but not causes; different perspectives interpret the same figures differently (interactionists focus on labelling processes; Marxists link gaps to material deprivation; feminists note gender patterns). The answer evaluates specific strengths and limitations in the context of educational attainment, cites at least two sociological perspectives or named theorists (e.g. Halsey on class barriers, Bowles and Gintis on correspondence principle), weighs evidence on both sides, and arrives at a supported conclusion.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present; both sides covered; named perspectives/sociologists referenced; a clear judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some named concepts; conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description of official statistics; few named sociologists; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
According to Walby, how many structures of patriarchy operate to restrict women's power in society?
A) Three
B) Four
C) Five
D) Six
practice_questions.marks: D) Six [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'patriarchy' as used by feminist sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that patriarchy refers to a system in which men hold power; 1 mark for clarifying that it is a structural or systemic concept in which women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions (not just that individual men dominate individual women). Example: 'Patriarchy is a structural system in which men hold dominant positions of power across social institutions — employment, the family, the state — and women are systematically disadvantaged as a result, regardless of formal legal equality.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the difference between private patriarchy and public patriarchy as described by Walby.
