practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Walby distinguished two historical forms of patriarchy. 2 marks for a developed description: 'Private patriarchy involves direct personal control of women by individual men — fathers or husbands — largely confining women to the domestic sphere with minimal access to public life, employment or legal rights. Public patriarchy characterises contemporary Western society: women have formal access to public life but are collectively disadvantaged within it — segregated into lower-paid occupations, under-represented in leadership, and subject to a persistent gender pay gap. Walby argues that while the form has changed, patriarchy continues to maintain male dominance.'

practice_questions.text: Describe two of Walby's six structures of patriarchy with evidence from contemporary UK society.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per structure. For each: 1 mark for correctly naming and briefly identifying the structure; 1 mark for a developed description with UK evidence. Paid work: women face the glass ceiling, the gender pay gap and concentration in lower-paid feminised occupations despite equality legislation. Household production: women carry a disproportionate share of unpaid domestic labour even when in full-time employment — the double shift. Patriarchal culture: double standards on women's behaviour in sexual conduct and public appearance. Sexuality: behaviour admired in men judged negatively in women. Male violence: fear of assault constrains women's behaviour in public spaces — Heidensohn. The state: under-representation in elected positions; equal pay laws weakly enforced.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that Walby's theory of patriarchy offers the best explanation of gender inequality in modern Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: Walby's six structures explained and illustrated with UK evidence — gender pay gap, glass ceiling, double shift, under-representation in leadership, Heidensohn on male violence. Private to public patriarchy shift explained. Evidence that inequality persists despite formal legal equality. Contrasting: functionalist view (gender role differences reflect functional specialisation; Parsons on expressive and instrumental roles); Marxist view (gender inequality serves capitalism; class conflict more fundamental). Named sociologists throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement offered.

Developing: Walby described but limited evaluation; minimal counter-perspective; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations of gender inequality in contemporary British society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Feminist/Walby analysis presented in depth — all six structures of patriarchy with UK evidence, private vs public patriarchy, persistence of inequality despite formal equality. At least two contrasting perspectives developed with equal depth: functionalist (Parsons on expressive and instrumental roles — gender differences as functional specialisation, not oppression); Marxist (gender inequality serves capitalism by providing unpaid domestic labour and a reserve army of flexible workers — class conflict is the fundamental explanation). Intersectionality point: gender interacts with class, ethnicity, age and disability — compounded disadvantage for women of colour, elderly women. Evidence weighed against each perspective. Supported judgement about whether Walby's framework, or a modified intersectional version of it, or a Marxist class-centred account, best explains gender inequality in contemporary Britain.

Secure: Walby explained with most arguments; contrasting perspective developed; judgement offered.

Developing: Walby described but limited comparison with other perspectives; weak evaluation; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of gender inequality; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which sampling method involves participants recruiting other members of the sample from their own networks?
A) Stratified sample
B) Quota sample
C) Systematic sample
D) Snowball sample
practice_questions.marks: D) Snowball sample [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'operationalisation' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying operationalisation as the process of turning abstract concepts into measurable terms. 1 mark for developing this: e.g. so that the concept can be investigated empirically, by specifying what indicator or measure will represent the concept in the research. Example: 'Operationalisation is the process of defining abstract sociological concepts (such as deprivation or exclusion) in concrete, measurable terms so they can be investigated, for example by using eligibility for free school meals as a measure of socioeconomic disadvantage.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one advantage of conducting a pilot study and describe how it would improve the quality of the research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. identifies ambiguous questions, reveals practical problems, checks timing, tests whether the sampling method is workable). 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying that a pilot study identifies ambiguous questions (1 mark) and explaining that if a question is unclear to respondents, different participants will interpret it differently, reducing the validity and reliability of the data; revising the question after the pilot ensures all participants understand it in the same way (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the key ethical issues a sociologist must address when researching youth offending, and explain one strategy for dealing with each.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Credit two well-explained ethical issues with a specific strategy each. Likely content: Informed consent (1 mark for identifying) — young offenders may be under 18, so parental or guardian consent must be obtained in addition to the participant's own agreement; the research purpose and right to withdraw must be explained clearly (1 mark for a specific strategy). Confidentiality (1 mark for identifying) — participants' identities must be anonymised in any published report and data stored securely so that their involvement cannot be traced; researchers must be clear that disclosures will not be reported to criminal justice agencies unless legal obligations arise (1 mark for strategy).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using participant observation to study gang culture among young people.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides addressed with named sociologists or methodological concepts, and a supported judgement. Advantages: generates rich, detailed qualitative data about how gang members understand their own behaviour; allows behaviour to be observed in natural settings rather than relying on self-report; avoids interviewer effect or questionnaire response bias; can access a hard-to-reach population that a snowball sample may not fully capture. Disadvantages: serious ethical risks (covert observation requires deception; consent may be impossible to obtain; researcher may witness criminal activity); personal danger to the researcher; the observer effect may change behaviour; findings are not generalisable from one gang to the wider population; time-consuming. Theoretical dimension: interactionists (Becker) favour qualitative methods that capture meanings from participants' perspectives; positivists would argue that observation produces data that cannot be statistically analysed. Student names at least one relevant methodological concept (triangulation, validity, reliability, observer effect) and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: both sides covered with relevant methodological vocabulary, judgement present. Developing: one-sided or underdeveloped. Emerging: basic points, little methodological reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that structured questionnaires are the most appropriate method for investigating patterns of youth offending in a local area.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two methodological concepts or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. For questionnaires: large samples can be reached quickly and cheaply; quantitative data allows statistical analysis and identification of patterns; can be anonymous, encouraging more honest disclosure of sensitive information; replicable (same questionnaire can be used in different areas or time periods for comparison). Against questionnaires: low response rates may bias the sample; questions are fixed in advance, missing unanticipated factors; crime is a sensitive topic and respondents may under-report; questionnaires assume literacy and language competence; they miss the meanings and experiences behind the patterns. Alternative methods: unstructured interviews or focus groups would provide richer data on why young people offend; participant observation would capture behaviour in natural settings but raises serious ethical issues; mixed methods with triangulation would combine pattern-finding and depth. Student discusses the match between method and research question, evaluates specific advantages and weaknesses in context, and reaches a supported conclusion. Secure: most arguments present, both sides covered, judgement reached. Developing: relevant points but mostly one-sided or underdeveloped. Emerging: basic points, mostly description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
A sociologist is given a table showing prosecution rates per 1,000 population for men (18.4) and women (4.2). What does this data show?
A) Men commit more crimes than women in absolute numbers
B) The prosecution rate for men is approximately 4 times higher than for women
C) Women are never prosecuted for serious offences
D) The dark figure of crime is larger for women than for men
practice_questions.marks: B) The prosecution rate for men is approximately 4 times higher than for women [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what sociologists mean by the term 'validity' in the context of research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating that validity refers to whether research measures what it claims to measure. 1 mark for developing this: e.g. a measure has high validity if it accurately reflects the social reality it is supposed to capture; crime statistics have low validity as a measure of true crime levels because of the dark figure of unreported and unrecorded offences. Example: 'Validity refers to whether a research instrument accurately measures what it claims to measure, so that findings reflect social reality rather than an artefact of the measurement process.'

practice_questions.text: A bar chart shows that recorded knife offences rose sharply between 2017 and 2022. Identify and describe one sociological reason for caution in interpreting this trend as evidence of a genuine increase in knife crime.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant reason for caution (e.g. changes in police recording practices; moral panic effects increasing reporting; the data is police-recorded, not a victim survey). 2 marks for a developed description. Example: The rise in recorded knife offences may partly reflect changes in police recording practices or increased public willingness to report following a media-driven moral panic (1). If media coverage of knife crime increased reporting and police attention, the rise in the recorded figures could reflect labelling and recording decisions rather than an actual increase in offending; comparing with Crime Survey for England and Wales data on knife crime victimisation over the same period would be needed to assess whether the trend reflects true change (2 marks for a developed, sociologically grounded point).

practice_questions.text: Describe how both the interactionist and Marxist perspectives would explain data showing that Black individuals are overrepresented in stop-and-search statistics.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per perspective. Interactionist: 1 mark for identifying that police use stereotyped labels and apply them selectively to Black young men; 1 mark for developing with Becker's labelling theory — stereotypes shape discretionary decisions about who to stop, so the data reflects labelling patterns rather than actual offending differences. Marxist: 1 mark for identifying institutional racism in the criminal justice system; 1 mark for developing with reference to the Macpherson Report (1999) finding of institutional racism in the Metropolitan Police, or with the argument that the bourgeoisie uses enforcement resources to control racialised and economically marginalised communities, reproducing racial and class inequality.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that sociologists should rely primarily on official statistics when investigating patterns of crime.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides addressed with named sociologists or methodological concepts, reaching a supported judgement. In support: official statistics are large-scale, nationally consistent and allow trend analysis over time; functionalists broadly accept them as useful indicators; they cover the entire population and allow group comparisons that small-scale studies cannot match. Against: the dark figure of crime means official statistics systematically under-represent offending; Marxist perspective argues they reflect policing priorities rather than harm; interactionist perspective (Becker) argues they measure labelling activity; feminist perspective argues crimes against women are especially undercounted; self-report and CSEW data challenge official patterns. Student names at least two perspectives or methodological concepts, presents both sides and reaches a supported judgement about whether official statistics should be primary or supplementary. Secure: both sides covered, named perspectives, judgement present. Developing: one-sided or underdeveloped. Emerging: basic points, little methodological reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effectively different sources of crime data allow sociologists to understand the true extent of crime in society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against each major data source, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. Police-recorded crime: strengths (historical depth, captures property crime, crime against organisations); limitations (dark figure, policing priorities, recording variation, Marxist and interactionist critiques). Crime Survey for England and Wales: strengths (independent of police, captures unreported crime, consistent over time); limitations (excludes murder, crimes against organisations, under-reports sensitive offences). Self-report studies: strengths (shows offending more evenly spread across groups, supports labelling theory); limitations (recall problems, social desirability bias, under-reporting of serious crime). Mixed methods / triangulation: combining sources reduces the limitations of each. Evaluation of reliability and validity of each source. Conclusion that no single source provides a complete picture; the sociologist must combine sources and apply critical awareness. Student names at least Becker or Chambliss alongside one structural perspective. Reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: most arguments present, both sides covered, judgement reached. Developing: relevant points but mostly descriptive, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists, little evaluation.
